item.title: Impossibility Results for Single-Cut Full-Open Card-Based Protocols with Any Number of Cards
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2960
Authors: Koji Nuida, Kazumasa Shinagawa, Yasuhide Numata
Summary: Card-based protocols are cryptographic protocols using a deck of physical cards instead of electronic computers, where information is encoded into a sequence of face-down cards and decoded by opening the cards, and random operations are realized by shuffles of cards. In this research area, there are known impossibility results for protocol construction, but most of the existing results (except for one result for a specific function under a non-standard encoding rule) are conditional on the number of cards used in a protocol, i.e., just giving lower bounds for the number of cards. In contrast, in this paper we give impossibility results, unconditional on the number of cards, for some kind of protocols computing wide classes of functions. Technically, our result is given by deepening a recently explored connection between card-based protocols and combinatorics on words.
Specifically, we consider card-based protocols with the following two properties: (1) just a single random cut is used as shuffles; (2) an opening operation is used just once, where all cards are opened at the same time. It has been known that an arbitrary function can be computed by slightly relaxing (1) to "a single shuffle" (not necessarily a random cut) or (2) to "a part of cards are opened". As opposed to them, in this paper we prove that for protocols satisfying both (1) and (2), for the case of symmetric Boolean functions and Boolean functions without redundant variables, the currently known protocols are essentially all of the possible cases; for any other function (in the sense of NPN non-equivalence), such a protocol is shown to be impossible regardless of the number of cards. We also partially extend the impossibility result to functions with non-binary outputs.

item.title: Classical Free-Start Collision Attacks on Full-Round AES-256-DM and AES-256-MMO
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2959
Authors: Liyuan Tang, Yanzhao Shen, Xiaoyang Dong
Summary: Despite extensive cryptanalysis of hash modes based on the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), no classical free-start collision attack has previously been reported for full-round AES-256-DM or AES-256-MMO. In this work, we address this problem by extending the guess-and-determine (GD) rebound methodology. Our main technical contribution is a precomputation-based method for handling conflicts involving guessed variables in the GD procedure. By precomputing solutions to the corresponding systems of byte equations, such conflicts can be resolved in $O(1)$ online time. We further exploit triangular dependencies among controllable guessed variables to reduce the memory required for precomputation.
Using this method, we construct classical free-start collision attacks applicable to both AES-256-DM and AES-256-MMO. For the full 14-round AES-256, the attacks require $2^{60}$ time and $2^{24}$ memory, providing the first classical free-start collision attacks on these full-round constructions. The same approach improves the time complexity of the full-round free-start differential $q$-multicollision attack from $q\cdot2^{67}$ to $q\cdot2^{60}$, with memory complexity $2^{24}$. We also obtain free-start collision attacks on the 12-round variants with time complexity $2^{54}$ and memory complexity $2^{24}$.

item.title: Classical Oracle Separation of QMA from the QCMA Hierarchy and Quantum Cryptography Even When P = QCMA
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2958
Authors: Alper Cakan
Summary: Remark. This work is in submission at STOC'27 and thus the full manuscript has been publicly posted on the conference website since November 3rd, 2026.
Inspired by the Codeword-Hash Structure problem recently introduced by Cakan (arXiV, 2026) to separate $\mathsf{QMA}$ from $\mathsf{QCIP}$, we introduce a new problem called Codeword-Hash pairs in Noise ($\mathsf{CHN}$) and prove that, in the query complexity model, it is in $\mathsf{QMA}$ but hard for the $\mathsf{QCMA}$ hierarchy $\mathsf{QCMAH} = \bigcup_{d\geq1}\mathsf{QCMA}^{\mathsf{QCMA}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{QCMA}}}}$, the classical-witness quantum-verifier analogue of $\mathsf{PH}=\bigcup_{d\ge1}\mathsf{NP}^{\mathsf{NP}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{NP}}}}$.
Using this problem, we show that there exists a classical oracle $\mathcal{O}$ such that $\mathsf{P}^{\mathcal{O}}=\mathsf{BQP}^{\mathcal{O}}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{\mathcal{O}} =\mathsf{QCMAH}^{\mathcal{O}} \subset \mathsf{QMA}^{\mathcal{O}} \text{ but } \mathsf{QMA}^{\mathcal{O}}\not\subseteq\mathsf{QCMAH}^{\mathcal{O}},$ thus showing that quantum state or quantum proof advantage could exist even if classical computers can efficiently solve any problem that can be quantumly verified with a classical proof.
Further, using our problem, we show that various quantum cryptographic primitives can exist even when $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{QCMA}$ and thus neither quantum-computable one-way functions nor (verifiable) quantum computational advantage exist. In more detail, we show that there exists a classical oracle $\mathcal{O}$ such that $\mathsf{P}^{\mathcal{O}} = \mathsf{BQP}^{\mathcal{O}} =\mathsf{QCMA}^{\mathcal{O}}=\mathsf{QCMAH}^{\mathcal{O}}$ but the following primitives exist relative to $\mathcal{O}$, answering an open question of Kretschmer, Qian, and Tal (STOC 2025).
(1) Pseudorandom states (PRS) with classical keys. (2) Pseudorandom functions (PRF) with (copy-protected) quantum secret keys, and thus also pseudorandom unitaries (PRU) with quantum secret keys, (3) Public-key encryption (PKE) with a (copy-protected) quantum decryption key, classical public keys and ciphertexts, (4) Signature schemes with quantum signing keys and either classical verification keys and quantum signatures or quantum verification keys and classical signatures, (5) Collusion-resistant public-key quantum money (PKQM) with classical verification keys.

item.title: Does Witness Indistinguishability Require Cryptography?
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2957
Authors: Gal Arnon, Noam Mazor, Rafael Pass, Jad Silbak
Summary: An interactive proof is witness indistinguishable ($\mathsf{WI}$) if the verifier cannot tell which of several valid witnesses the prover used. $\mathsf{WI}$ is a fundamental privacy guarantee that is implied by a number of central primitives, including zero knowledge ($\mathsf{ZK}$), batch arguments, and succinct arguments.
Ostrovsky and Wigderson [OW93] showed that, assuming the worst-case hardness of $\mathsf{NP}$, $\mathsf{ZK}$ proofs for $\mathsf{NP}$ imply auxiliary-input one-way functions. This was recently strengthened by Hirahara and Nanashima [HN24], who showed that, under the same assumption, $\mathsf{ZK}$ proofs for $\mathsf{NP}$ imply standard one-way functions. For $\mathsf{WI}$, no analogous result was known; in fact, we do not known if cryptography is necessary for $\mathsf{WI}$ at all.
One source of difficulty in proving a cryptographic implication from $\mathsf{WI}$ is the possible unconditional existence of witness canonicalization. More formally, an $\varepsilon$-witness canonicalization ($\varepsilon$-$\mathsf{WC}$) is a deterministic polynomial-time map that sends any valid witness $w$ for $x$, together with public randomness $r$, to an efficiently verifiable string that depends only on $x$ and $r$ (and not on the specific witness $w$), except with probability $\varepsilon$. Completeness and soundness hold perfectly (only canonicalization is allowed to fail). Indeed, if a valid witnesses for an $\mathsf{NP}$ statement can be efficiently mapped to a single canonical representation, then $\mathsf{WI}$ is trivial and requires no cryptography: the prover sends the canonical witness, and so reveals nothing about its own.
We prove the following:
1. Let $L$ be an $\mathsf{NP}$ language that admits no $\varepsilon$-$\mathsf{WC}$ for some inverse-polynomial $\varepsilon$. Then, under a derandomization assumption, every constant-round (honest-verifier) $\mathsf{WI}$ proof for $L$ implies infinitely-often auxiliary-input one-way functions. The derandomization assumption can be avoided if one settles for canonicalization with negligible completeness and soundness errors.
2. Combining (a variant of) the above with a theorem of Bitansky, Kamath, Paneth, Rothblum, and Vasudevan [BKPRV24] yields analogous consequences for sufficiently compressing batch arguments and succinct non-interactive arguments.
Since it is unlikely that $\mathsf{SAT}$ has a $\varepsilon$-$\mathsf{WC}$, even for constant $\varepsilon$, the above results establish that cryptography is necessary for designing $\mathsf{WI}$ proofs (or sufficiently compressing BARG/SNARGs) for $\mathsf{SAT}$. As far as we are aware, these are the first results establishing the necessity of cryptographic hardness for witness indistinguishability, BARGs, and SNARGs.

item.title: Complexity-Theoretic Consequences of Zero-Knowledge with Inefficient Simulation
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2956
Authors: Gal Arnon, Noam Mazor, Rafael Pass, Jad Silbak
Summary: Zero-knowledge ($\mathsf{ZK}$) protocols are one of the most fundamental cryptographic primitives. Classic results in the 1980s established that one-way functions (OWFs) suffice for constructing $\mathsf{ZK}$ for $\mathsf{NP}$ (Goldreich-Micali-Wigderson [JACM'91], Naor [CRYPTO’89], Hastad et al. [SICOMP’99]). Moreover, OWFs are, in fact, necessary for $\mathsf{ZK}$ for $\mathsf{NP}$, due to the classic result of Ostrovsky and Wigderson [ISTCS'93], which was recently strengthened by Hirahara and Nanashima [STOC'24].
But for many applications of $\mathsf{ZK}$, it suffices to consider a slight relaxation of the $\mathsf{ZK}$ property where the simulator is allowed to run in super-polynomial time (Pass [Eurocrypt'03]). Surprisingly, the results of Ostrovsky and Wigderson break once we allow even a slightly inefficient simulator. Indeed, a recent result by Baril and Haitner [CRYPTO'26] shows that, without efficient simulation, $\mathsf{ZK}$ does not imply one-way functions in a black-box manner.
We show that two-message arguments with a (non-trivial) inefficient simulator imply the errorless average-case hardness of the Minimum Time-Bounded Kolmogorov Complexity Problem ($\mathsf{MKtP}$) over the uniform distribution. The hardness of the same problem against two-sided error algorithms is known to imply OWFs (Liu and Pass, [FOCS'20]).
As far as we know, this result is the first complexity-theoretic consequence of $\mathsf{ZK}$ with even just slightly super-polynomial-time simulation.

item.title: A Note on the Unforgeability Hierarchy of Non-Interactive Threshold Signatures, with a Mechanisation in EasyCrypt
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2955
Authors: João Diogo Duarte
Summary: Bellare et al. (CRYPTO 2022) define a hierarchy of unforgeability notions for non-interactive threshold signatures, TS-UF-0 to TS-UF-4 and TS-SUF-2 to TS-SUF-4. They prove that each notion implies the weaker ones and that TS-UF-0 implies TS-UF-1 with a loss of $\binom{ns}{t-1}$ for $ns$ servers and threshold $t$, and they separate every other pair of notions. Cremers, Peltonen and Zhao (2024) showed that TS-UF-4 does not imply TS-UF-3, and Bellare, Tessaro and Zhu revised the definitions in response. We give machine-checked proofs in EasyCrypt of the revised hierarchy, of the loose implication from TS-UF-0 to TS-UF-1, and of the attacks behind the separations. We also prove that the loss of $\binom{ns}{t-1}$ is optimal for an implication that holds for every scheme, up to the security of a signature scheme.

item.title: Concretely Efficient Byzantine Agreement and Interactive Consistency for Honest Majority
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2954
Authors: Michele Ciampi, Pouyan Forghani, Yun Lu, Vassilis Zikas
Summary: We consider two of the main notions of round-efficient Byzantine agreement (BA): expected constant rounds and early stopping. Randomized protocols can terminate in an expected constant number of rounds, while early-stopping protocols terminate in a number of rounds that depends only on the actual number $f\le t$ of corrupted parties. Recent works achieve both guarantees at once, but at a high concrete cost: assuming PKI, for the optimal threshold $t2$, the previous protocol with the smallest expected round complexity needs $37$ rounds in expectation and $15f+29$ in the worst case.
In this work, we present a BA protocol for $t2$, secure against an adaptive adversary assuming a PKI, that terminates in $18$ rounds in expectation and in at most $8f+18$ rounds in the worst case. Moreover, our protocol has the following optimistic feature: if no party is corrupted and all inputs agree, every party outputs after a single round. Our protocol is natively multi-valued and does not rely on random oracles. At the core of our result is a new randomized BA protocol in which a successful leader election leads to agreement within the same phase.
We extend our results to Byzantine broadcast, obtaining a protocol that has $19$ rounds in expectation and $8f+19$ in the worst case, and to interactive consistency (IC), retaining the same round complexity while providing an optimistic fast path in which all parties output after only 2 rounds when everyone is honest. We do so by directly parallelizing our BB protocol, instead of using a generic IC compiler, for which, at $t<n/2$, the best known bounds are more than $4000$ rounds in expectation and $184f+730$ in the worst case.

item.title: Fuzzy Private Set Intersection with Large Databases via Locality-Sensitive Hashing
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2953
Authors: Francesca Falzon, Andreas Athanasiou, Laura Hetz, Tjitske Ollie Koster, Evangelia Anna Markatou
Summary: Many query workloads require privacy-preserving similarity joins: parties, each holding a private database, may want to learn which of their records are close to records in the other party's database under a distance metric, without leaking anything beyond this information. Fuzzy private set intersection (fuzzy PSI) is a cryptographic primitive that addresses this problem. In this setting, a client and a server hold sets $X$ and $Y$, respectively, and the client learns the subset of points in $X$ that are "close" to points in $Y$. Fuzzy PSI has many use cases, including biometric authentication, password breach monitoring, contact tracing, regional-outbreak monitoring, and machine-learning label matching. Despite growing interest in fuzzy PSI, many existing schemes still require communication costs and client computation linear in the server's set size $|Y|$. Consequently, these protocols do not scale well to the unbalanced setting, where $|X| \ll |Y|$, as is common in many client-to-server applications.
In this work, we propose an efficient fuzzy PSI protocol for the unbalanced setting. At its core is a fuzzy probabilistic data structure (fuzzy PDS), which generalizes prior work by combining locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) with compact filters, enabling tunable false-positive and false-negative rates while ensuring efficient queries. Building on techniques from unbalanced PSI, we combine oblivious pseudorandom functions and private information retrieval with our fuzzy PDS to support private and communication-efficient approximate matching. We instantiate the protocol with an LSH for the $L_2$ metric and evaluate it on two real-world workloads: regional-outbreak monitoring and machine-learning label matching. Our results show significant reductions in communication and runtime compared with state-of-the-art fuzzy PSI schemes, with gains that increase as the server database size $|Y|$ grows.

item.title: Beyond Leaderless: Randomized Consensus Against Mobile Crashes
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2952
Authors: Ittai Abraham, Kaya Alpturer, Pranav Garimidi, Joachim Neu, Tim Roughgarden, Ertem Nusret Tas
Summary: Many consensus protocols fail to terminate under attack from an adversary that has the power to move between replicas and repeatedly crash one of them, even in synchrony. We present Multi-Leader Fixed-View Simplex (ML-FVS) to defend against such an adversary while keeping the simple structure and good-case latency of Simplex consensus. Our protocol extends fixed-view Simplex with multiple leaders, each of which may broadcast a proposal. At the voting deadline, each replica votes on the set of proposals it has seen so far. A hidden threshold beacon revealed after the votes gives a priority order on the multiple leaders, resolving each vote to its highest-priority proposal. Our model combines permanent adaptive Byzantine faults with mobile crashes. For a constant crash budget and Δ-delayed Byzantine corruption, we obtain O(Δ) expected latency over repeated views whose leaders start honest. With immediate Byzantine corruptions, the protocol still achieves liveness. We also evaluate the protocol under random network delays and stochastic faults, finding that multiple leaders reduce view failures even when rational leaders delay their proposals to increase rewards.

item.title: SoK: A Unified Framework for Analyzing Coercion Resistance in Electronic Voting
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2951
Authors: Wonseok Choi, Won Kim, Changmin Lee
Summary: Electronic voting (E-voting) can improve the accessibility and efficiency of elections, but its reliance on electronic systems also introduces security and privacy threats. In remote e-voting, adversaries may observe voters' behavior and obtain some electronic information, making voters more vulnerable to coercion. Hence, coercion resistance is a security property of e-voting protocols which ensures that a voter can deviate from an adversary’s instructions. However, existing e-voting protocols establish coercion resistance under different assumptions about the protocol settings, such as election environments, trust assumptions, and adversarial capabilities. In particular, e-voting protocols involve diverse procedures and interactions, resulting in different protocol syntaxes. Consequently, it is difficult to determine whether their coercion resistance guarantees hold in practical election settings and which protocols provide stronger protection against coercion.
In this work, we present a unified framework for systematically analyzing coercion resistance across different e-voting protocols. We introduce a unified syntax for e-voting protocols that captures diverse coercion-resistant protocols. This syntax provides a common execution model in which adversarial capabilities can be specified consistently across different protocols. Using our syntax, we systematically express existing protocols within this framework. We also adapt standard definitions of verifiability and ballot privacy of e-voting protocols to our syntax. Using these definitions, we compare the verifiability and ballot privacy of existing coercion-resistant e-voting protocols.
We then extend existing definitions of coercion resistance to our unified e-voting syntax. We systematically classify coercion-resistance settings along five axes: corruption bounds, corruption modes, coercion phases, timing restrictions, and the number of coercion interactions. We establish implication relations among the resulting coercion resistance notions to characterize their relative strength. Using this classification, we evaluate existing e-voting protocols by proving the maximality of coercer-capability settings under which each protocol achieves coercion resistance. Our framework thereby enables direct and fine-grained comparison of coercion-resistant e-voting protocols under our common model.

item.title: LNRPIR: High Throughput PIR with Flexible Communication-Computation Trade-offs
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2950
Authors: Liren Xu, Zhe Li
Summary: Private information retrieval (PIR) is a powerful cryptographic primitive with numerous applications. Recent works have largely pursued two different directions: minimizing online communication at the expense of high online computation costs, or achieving high server throughput while incurring substantial online communication overhead. In this work, we introduce LNRPIR, a PIR scheme that achieves high server throughput with moderate online communication overhead. LNRPIR also provides flexible trade-offs between communication and computation, addressing a gap in the trade-off space left by prior works. Our evaluation shows that LNRPIR retrieves a $256$-byte record from an $8$ GB database $2.541\times$ faster than VIA-C (S&P 2026), a state-of-the-art protocol in the client-hint model, with only $10.473$ KB of online communication. Furthermore, compared with InsPIRe (S&P 2026), a state-of-the-art protocol in the silent-preprocessing model, LNRPIR achieves $17.074\times$ lower online communication overhead for an $8$ GB database, while incurring only $1.885\times$ the online computation time of InsPIRe. LNRPIR primarily relies on three novel ciphertext conversion techniques: LWE-to-NTRU conversion, LWE-to-VNTRU conversion, and NTRU-to-RLWE conversion.

item.title: Homogeneous rotation symmetric bent functions in twelve variables are quadratic
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2949
Authors: Filipe Martins Vono, André Oliveira Naufel de Toledo, Valéria Gonzaga Santos
Summary: Every homogeneous rotation symmetric bent Boolean function in twelve variables is quadratic. There are exactly sixteen such functions in labelled coordinates. The main step is to rule out degree four. The proof groups inputs according to which opposite coordinates agree. Walsh divisibility forces the restriction to each group to be quadratic. The squared Walsh sums of these restrictions must then fit a fixed total. This rules out one of the three possible restrictions on the diagonal and severely limits the other two. Explicit polynomial identities exclude the remaining possibilities. The classification and the coefficient characterization were formally verified in Lean 4.36.0. The appended supplement gives the identities, the case coverage, and instructions for verifying the calculations.

item.title: LaTSEC: Lattice-Based Threshold Signatures with Native Non-Interactive Identifiable Abort and Compact Per-Party Storage
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2948
Authors: Muhammad Arzaki, Muhammed F. Esgin, Markku-Juhani O. Saarinen, Amin Sakzad, Ron Steinfeld
Summary: We present $\mathsf{LaTSEC}$, a three-round lattice-based threshold signature scheme with native non-interactive identifiable abort. Each party holds one small-norm signing share and is associated with one public abort key, against which its partial signature is verified directly, without zero-knowledge proofs or an additional interactive protocol. Prior lattice-based threshold signatures that identify misbehaving parties rely on one of three mechanisms: zero-knowledge proofs, an additional interactive protocol, or an everywhere-short secret sharing scheme in which each party holds multiple signing shares, each with its own public abort key. Compared with schemes that use the third mechanism, $\mathsf{LaTSEC}$ substantially reduces per-party storage. The construction uses $\mathsf{SEC}$, a recent ramp everywhere-short secret sharing scheme based on lossless expanders that gives each party a single short share. We prove correctness, identifiable-abort security, and threshold unforgeability under the standard $\mathsf{MLWE}$ and $\mathsf{MSIS}$ assumptions. The unforgeability proof introduces the Repeated-$\boldsymbol{A}$ Matrix Hint-MLWE problem, a new variant of $\mathsf{MLWE}$ with hints that captures the complete tuple of correlated public abort keys. We rigorously prove that this new variant admits a reduction from the standard $\mathsf{MLWE}$ problem. For 60 parties at 128-bit security, $\mathsf{LaTSEC}$ tolerates up to 6 corrupted parties, and, empirically, a randomly chosen set of at least 46 parties can sign with probability at least 0.99. Each party holds one signing share of about 14.3 KiB and is associated with one 24-KiB public abort key.

item.title: SPECTRA: Sensor Provenance and Execution Through Recursive Arguments
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2947
Authors: Marco Calipari, Paul Timke Contreras, Mohammad Hamad, Sebastian Steinhorst
Summary: Autonomous systems plan and act on sensor data, yet existing integrity measures protect that data only after it has been produced. Signature- or proof-based schemes trust every processing stage that runs prior to the protection, so an attacker with privileged access can manipulate the data before any cryptographic measure applies. We propose SPECTRA, a novel, general sensor model that moves the trust boundary as close as possible to the analog domain while attesting every stage in the digital domain. We formally define the SPECTRA sensor by leveraging the recursive arguments of Non-uniform Incrementally Verifiable Computation (NIVC), define when a stage is attested, with the resulting trust boundary, and compare it to the state of the art, identifying a trust gap, where current solutions protect a single stage, or trust the whole sensor until the data leaves it. Furthermore, we instantiate SPECTRA for the camera pipeline (SPECTRA-CAM), with Bayer-compliant step circuit implementation, and evaluate it on CPU and GPU, from an embedded NVIDIA Jetson to high- end server hardware, over a wide range of frame sizes. Finally, we expose the limitations of the state of the art with Pipeline Ordering Shuffling Attacks, showing that merely reordering the pipeline stages can mislead downstream classifiers while the output still carries a valid signature. In the context of this attack we show why the state of the art falls short, and motivate the need to rethink sensor attestation from a data-centric perspective. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first image pipeline proven with NIVC, optionally in zero-knowledge, and the first image-based proof system evaluated directly on commodity embedded hardware, the NVIDIA Jetson, which proves frames up to 4K in under 6 GiB of memory. With GPU acceleration, its proving time on utility frame sizes is on average 3.1× lower than on its CPU, and on classifier-sized frames it stays within tens of seconds of server-grade hardware.

item.title: BOCCHI: Compact Blind SNARK via Malformation-Tolerant Ciphertext Aggregation
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2946
Authors: Ye Yu, Kexi Huang
Summary: Blind SNARKs combine fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) with cryptographic proofs to enable verifiable computation over encrypted data, and can substantially outperform SNARK-over-FHE approaches in efficiency. However, ciphertext openings in existing constructions can inflate proofs to tens or hundreds of megabytes. We present BOCCHI, a compact and efficient blind SNARK that addresses this bottleneck by committing to ciphertexts natively and opening them through a few aggregates. To establish soundness even for malformed ciphertexts, we introduce canonical binding and a lightweight noise filter that achieves it with optimal error, tools that may be of independent interest. We further formulate this transformation as a Commit–Aggregate–Check (CAC) compiler and show its effectiveness on two systems with different PIOPs (GKR and Fractal). At $2^{22}$ constraints, BOCCHI produces a 6.57 MB proof in 115.3 seconds, 9.3× smaller and 2.54× faster than Phalanx. Its proof is the smallest among five baselines. Our implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/BOCCHI-Artifacts.

item.title: Generic Construction of Public-key Encryption with Bidirectional Keyword Search
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2945
Authors: Riku Matsui, Keita Emura
Summary: Public-key Encryption with Bidirectional Keyword Search (PEBKS), proposed by Zhang, Qin, Dong, and Tian (Computer Standards & Interfaces, 2021), extends the functionality of Public-key Encryption with Keyword Search (PEKS) by allowing not only the receiver but also the sender to generate trapdoors for keyword search. In this paper, we identify a close relationship between PEBKS and Public-key Authenticated Encryption with Keyword Search (PAEKS). Leveraging the generic construction of PAEKS proposed by Li and Boyen (IACR Communications in Cryptology, 2024), which is based on Non-Interactive Key Exchange (NIKE) and symmetric-key Equality Predicate Encryption (EPE), we show that PEBKS can also be generically constructed from the same building blocks. While Zhang et al. proposed a concrete pairing-based PEBKS scheme, our generic construction yields PEBKS instantiations under a wide range of cryptographic assumptions, including pairing-free Diffie-Hellman assumptions, lattices, isogenies, and codes. Furthermore, we define Key Collision Resistance for EPE as a new security property required for proving Consistency of PEBKS. We prove that the Li-Boyen EPE construction based on a pseudorandom function (PRF) achieves this property if the underlying PRF is Key Collision Resistant. We also discuss the use of AES and HMAC as the underlying PRF in light of the key collision attack reported by Taiyama et al. (Asiacrypt 2024). Since Key Collision Resistance is likewise required for proving Consistency of PAEKS, our result complements the Li-Boyen generic construction of PAEKS and is of independent interest.

item.title: Linear Cryptanalysis of ISO Standard SEED: Exact Trail Optima via Divide-and-Decide Search
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2944
Authors: Haonan Hong, Kai Zhang
Summary: SEED is a block cipher developed by the Korea Information Security Agency (KISA) and standardized in ISO/IEC 18033-3. For more than two decades, its best linear cryptanalysis has remained KISA's evaluation: a 5-round distinguisher and no key-recovery attack.
In this paper, a new hierarchical certified search framework, called divide-and-decide (D&D), is proposed to determine exact optima of linear trails rather than heuristic upper bounds. D&D divides the trail space at two levels, followed by one decision. At the pattern level, the trail space is partitioned by the positions of trivial rounds, and whole patterns are eliminated before any solver call by the F-function spacing bound (FSB) for SEED, an analytic lower bound. At the layer level, each remaining pattern is divided into layers of integer cost, and the lowest layers are enumerated with a satisfiability (SAT) solver to obtain an incumbent trail. At the decision level, the weight beyond the integer cost is treated as an excess, and each remaining layer is closed by a single SAT decision model on this excess instead of being enumerated. For SEED, D&D gives the exact 3- to 7-round optima 18.830, 33.541, 43.472, 55.027, and 65.220, and shows that every 16-round trail has weight at least 112.980. The 6-round hull of weight 53.168 leads to the first linear key-recovery attack on 7-round SEED, and the 7-round hull of weight 63.391 extends linear distinguishers within the codebook from 5 to 7 rounds.

item.title: A Transparent Post-Quantum Zero-Knowledge Argument for R1CS
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2943
Authors: Vu Hung Tung
Summary: We construct a transparent, post-quantum zero-knowledge argument of knowledge for R1CS. Satisfiability of $n$ constraints is reduced by two masked sumchecks to linear claims on a committed short vector; every field element the prover reveals is uniform. The witness is committed row-wise with Module-SIS (Ajtai) commitments; evaluation claims are proven by folding the rows with monomial challenges, whose differences have short scaled inverses, so that the extraction norm grows only singly exponentially in the folding depth. The row commitments and partial evaluations are moved into the witness of a LaBRADOR proof and replaced by two short outer commitments, so the proof has size polylogarithmic in $n$. The verifier runs in time $\tilde O(\sqrt n)\cdot\mathrm{poly}(\lambda)$ plus $T_\mathrm{circ}$, the time to evaluate the multilinear extensions of the constraint matrices, which we bound for data-parallel circuits. We prove completeness, knowledge soundness of the interactive protocol, and classical zero-knowledge in the programmable random-oracle model, and give parameters from a Core-SVP estimate. The concrete verifier cost at $n=2^{20}$ exceeds that of checking the circuit directly; the gain is asymptotic. Soundness of the Fiat--Shamir compiled protocol and a quantum-oracle zero-knowledge bound are not proven.

item.title: Differential–Linear Distinguisher Search via Walsh Spectra over Low-Dimensional Mask Subspaces
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2942
Authors: Chenlu Zheng, Liu Zhang, Zilong Wang
Summary: Searching for differential--linear (DL) distinguishers in ARX and AND--RX ciphers often requires empirical evaluation of multi-round middle correlations. Hourglass(-like) structures provide effective guidance by restricting middle differences and output masks to sparse forms. However, the corresponding low-weight output-mask position need not be the most favorable boundary for empirical middle-correlation evaluation. Exploring alternative boundaries may involve multi-bit output masks, whose numerous possible combinations make empirical evaluation expensive.
We propose a spectral DL search framework for efficiently evaluating multiple middle output masks. We use Hamming-weight-one correlations to select low-dimensional output-mask subspaces and apply the fast Walsh--Hadamard transform to jointly evaluate all masks in each selected subspace using shared samples. Experiments on 32-bit ciphers show that HW1-guided subspaces can recover DL candidates with correlation estimates comparable to those obtained through full-state spectral evaluation. We integrate this approach with round-split selection, automated outer-trail search, and independent fixed-key evaluation of the retained middle correlations. Experiments on SIMON, SIMECK, SPECK, and CHAM yield DL distinguishers with improved round coverage or estimated correlations. In particular, we obtain a 36-round SIMON128 distinguisher under single-trail outer-component evaluation and a 39-round result through refined outer-component evaluation. Our results further show that evaluating multi-bit masks at alternative middle-output boundaries can reveal more readily detectable correlations or reduce reliance on single-trail approximations.

item.title: Recovery Attacks on Distance-Preserving Encrypted Vector Databases
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2941
Authors: Chen Gong, Xiangyu Wang, Dan Zhu, Bowen Zhao, Jie Li, Xinghua Li, Jianfeng Ma
Summary: Private retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems based on distance-comparison-preserving encryption (DCPE) are widely adopted in industry to protect sensitive embeddings while maintaining low-latency search. However, DCPE inherently leaks the relational geometry of stored embeddings by preserving relative distance comparisons across ciphertexts, making its security in practical deployments questionable. This paper demonstrates that the geometric structure DCPE preserves to enable nearest-neighbor search directly exposes the underlying data manifold to full database recovery from snapshots. We introduce two practical recovery attacks: (1) Attack A, which requires only a leaked snapshot, the public encoder, and an auxiliary candidate corpus, achieving 100\% record re-identification; and (2) Attack B, which requires no candidate corpus and uses a single known plaintext-ciphertext pair to resolve the secret scale in DCPE, reconstructing embeddings with 0.997 mean cosine similarity and restoring a functional search index. Furthermore, our evaluation indicates that existing defensive countermeasures offer minimal protection. Crucially, full-database reconstruction is computationally efficient, incurring an execution overhead that is even lower than that of the original encryption pass. Therefore, leaked DCPE snapshots must be treated as plaintext disclosures, underscoring the urgent need to explore and adopt truly secure cryptographic alternatives for private RAG.

item.title: Short-Input Random Oracles (and PRFs) over Abelian Groups: New Generalisations and Better Bounds
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2940
Authors: Ritam Bhaumik
Summary: At Eurocrypt '26, Bhaumik et al. initiated a systematic study of short-input random oracles built from public random permutations over $\mathbb{Z}_2^n$. While their main focus was on length-preserving random oracles, they also proved that XORP, the expanding construction at the core of CENC (Iwata, FSE '06), is indifferentiable from a random function up to about $N^{2/3}$ queries for a permutation with domain size $N$ ($= 2^n$). We extend this study in several directions. For classifying short-input expanding random oracles, we introduce GXP, a family of constructions that use independent random permutations over an arbitrary abelian group of order $N$ to build a function with several output blocks, each the difference of two masked permutation outputs. GXP covers XORP with one or several permutations, LXoP (Dinur, Eurocrypt '25), and the widely-studied sum of two permutations.
We study the security of GXP in both keyless and keyed settings. In the keyless setting, a recent preprint from Kim has shown that the sum of two permutations over $\mathbb{Z}_2^n$ with a class of simulators called uniform simulators achieves a tight indifferentiability from a random oracle up to about $N^{3/4}$ queries. We build on this analysis, and prove that every member of GXP, over every finite abelian group, with arbitrary automorphism masks (under an extra width condition for some singular masks) and with unused permutation inputs, is indifferentiable up to about $N^{3/4}$ queries, for a uniform simulator with three trials and an acceptance coin. For admissible masks we give a sharper bound with explicit constants; other masks only add lower-order terms. The coin is necessary: without it, the simulator is distinguishable at about $N^{2/3}$ queries. Extending Kim's attack, with coset progressions in place of subgroups, we show that the exponent $3/4$ is tight for this simulator, for every family whose construction domain has density bounded below.
In the keyed setting, we extend the Fourier-analytic method put forward by Bhaumik et al. in another recent preprint, and establish the pseudorandomness with advantage $O_w(q/N^{3/2})$ for every rigid-free member of GXP, with explicit constants and over every finite abelian group. Pseudorandomness is thus governed by rigid-freeness, a strengthening of admissibility: rigid pairs and non-admissible masks can both limit it to about $q/N$, while neither affects the indifferentiability exponent.
The fork constructions ForkEDMD and ForkCENC of Dutta et al., and EDMD, in which the output of one permutation call becomes the input of all the other calls, are not members of GXP. A change of variables on the permutations turns each of them into a member with exactly the same security, so all our results apply to them as well.

item.title: Anonymous C2PA: Feasibility of Large-Scale Anonymous Image Provenance
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2939
Authors: Kelsey Merrill, Sarah Scheffler
Summary: High-quality AI-generated images are easy to create and near-indistinguishable from real photos, heightening the need to reliably establish image authenticity. The Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) has developed a technical standard under which cameras and editing software cryptographically sign the images they create, along with metadata and edit history. The standard is widely deployed in products by Google, Sony, Adobe, and others. However, C2PA offers no anonymity for signers. Signed images can be linked to a specific device or person, creating serious surveillance risks. C2PA also lacks formal security definitions, making it difficult for other systems to build on it with provable guarantees.
We formalize C2PA v2.5, and then we derive and formalize security and privacy properties desirable for an ideal anonymous image provenance system. Our primary building block for formalization is ring signatures, which let users sign on behalf of a group while staying anonymous within it. We give a new construction of shrinkable ring signatures that supports arbitrary subrings; this can be used to revoke compromised keys by "shrinking'' these keys out of existing signatures. Prior work supported only a small, fixed set of subrings.
In our formalization, we find that several desiderata for an anonymous image provenance system are fundamentally incompatible. In particular, we prove that shrinking ring signatures requires work linear in the number of signatures shrunk, and in some settings, linear-sized public evidence; both are impractical at a global scale. We then explore the resulting trade-off space and analyze candidate systems making different choices among the strength of authenticity guarantees, network access requirements, and post-quantum security. Our work answers calls for a more private image provenance system and identifies several paths toward practical solutions.

item.title: Post-Quantum Adaptive Multiparty NIKE
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2938
Authors: Shafik Nassar, Brent Waters
Summary: Non-interactive key exchange (NIKE) is a fundamental cryptographic primitive that enables a group of users to establish a shared secret key without any interaction. Constructing multiparty NIKE for groups larger than three has proven notoriously difficult, with all known constructions requiring indistinguishability obfuscation (iO) or multilinear maps. A major challenge in this area is achieving adaptive security, where the adversary chooses the target set of users after observing the system's public keys and can dynamically corrupt honest users, without incurring a sub-exponential loss in the security reduction. The only known construction up to this point has been that of Koppula, Waters, and Zhandry (TCC 2022), which relied on polynomially secure iO and a q-type assumption over pairing-free groups.
In this work, we present the first adaptively secure multiparty NIKE schemes from standard, static, and post-quantum polynomial assumptions. More broadly, we develop new techniques that allow us to construct adaptive multiparty NIKE from polynomially secure iO and either of Ring LWE, DDH or even cryptographic group actions. Specifically, we introduce a new abstraction called Key-Accumulative PRFs (KA-PRFs), which captures the structure common to all of the aforementioned algebraic assumptions, and construct our NIKE scheme from polynomially secure KA-PRFs and polynomially secure iO.
Our scheme supports an unbounded number of honest and malicious users, where the party size and the number of dynamic corruptions are fixed at setup.

item.title: Any Friend of Yours: Asynchronous Consensus with Unknown Participants from Local Trust
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2937
Authors: Ignacio Amores-Sesar, Simon Holmgaard Kamp, Juan Villacis
Summary: Byzantine agreement protocols typically assume that all processes already agree on who participates and which failures must be tolerated. In an open system, reaching agreement on this information is itself a consensus problem. We avoid this circularity by presenting asynchronous protocols in which each process acts only on its own local trust. Each process declares quorums over the identities it knows and communicates by authenticated multicast. Processes need not know the number of participants or the trust assumptions of others, and we assume no trusted dealer, common reference string, or bound on the number of identities, including Sybil identities. Unlike Stellar and prior asymmetric-trust protocols, our protocols do not require a closed set of mutually trusting correct processes. Instead, their guarantees are characterized by depth, a fine-grained, failure-dependent measure of how well each process's trust matches the actual failures.
We construct validated reliable broadcast, Byzantine agreement, agreement on a core set, and state machine replication in this model. The main technical ingredient for randomized termination is an approximate common coin based only on local trust.

item.title: Aggregating ML-DSA Signatures Without Recursion: A Cross-Field Argument for the Commitment Hash
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2936
Authors: Jipeng Zhang, Jiaheng Zhang
Summary: Consensus protocols must compress tens of thousands of signatures per block, yet ML-DSA (FIPS 204) signatures are kilobytes long and lack native aggregation. Aerie aggregates Falcon signatures into a single succinct proof per batch without recursion, using a sum-check-based polynomial interactive oracle proof (PIOP) over the Akita lattice-based polynomial commitment. Extending this approach to ML-DSA is challenging: the hash that its verifier recomputes from the response and hint takes seven Keccak-f permutations, or nine for ML-DSA-87, which are expensive over prime fields.
We address this bottleneck by proving ML-DSA's algebraic and Boolean components over separate fields, supporting all three FIPS 204 parameter sets. A PIOP over a 64-bit prime field handles the lattice relation, hint verification, and range checks, while Flock proves Keccak over GF(2). We introduce a cross-field parity bridge to enforce bitwise consistency between the two commitments. Using seeded sparse matrices, the bridge detects any fixed nonzero difference except with probability below 2^-144.6, independently of batch size. The aggregate certifies that every signature passes FIPS 204 verification. In the classical random-oracle model, each Fiat-Shamir challenge incurs at most 2^-128 soundness error per query, as in Aerie, and aggregate unforgeability reduces to the strong unforgeability of ML-DSA.
On 16 AMD Zen 5 cores with AVX2, our prover aggregates 32,768 ML-DSA-44 signatures in 2.68 s, at 49.2 bytes per signature. For ML-DSA-87, it takes 4.13 s at 82.7 bytes per signature. Against the Johnson-regime variant of Alloul26, a prime-field ML-DSA-87 aggregator, our prover is 43x faster and our aggregates are 1.8x smaller.

item.title: A Key Recovery Attack on TRIKE Based on Decoding Failures
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2935
Authors: Alessandro Annechini, Alessandro Barenghi, Gerardo Pelosi
Summary: TRIKE is a code-based Key Encapsulation Mechanism submitted to the Next-Generation Commercial Cryptographic algorithms (NGCC) standardization program currently run in People's Republic of China. TRIKE, similarly to other Quasi Cyclic Moderate Density Parity Check (QC-MDPC) code-based KEMs such as BIKE, is built with a decryption procedure which recovers a sparse error vector (i.e., the message) given its syndrome (i.e., the ciphertext) through a secret sparse parity-check matrix, employing an iterative bit-flipping decoder. Differently from BIKE, TRIKE employs a QC-MDPC matrix with a different structure, allowing them to improve the decoding, and hence the decryption, time. In order to guarantee IND-CCA security, the code length is chosen in order to reduce the Decoding Failure Rate (DFR) below $2^{-\lambda}$, where $\lambda$ is the bit security level; such a DFR is estimated with extrapolation techniques. In this work, we show that the QC-MDPC codes employed in TRIKE are affected by the so-called near codewords phenomenon. We provide a lower bound on the DFR given by such near codewords, showing that the DFR of TRIKE is significantly higher than the required value for all parameter sets. This alone constitutes a breach of IND-CCA security requirements. We propose a key recovery attack based on near codeword-induced decoding failures. For NGCC security level $1$, $\lambda=128$, the attack requires less than $2^{80}$ (random) ciphertexts and lowers the hardness of the static key recovery step down to $2^{65.52}$ bit operations. We validate our attack strategy and complexity estimation on a toy parameter set with extrapolated DFR below $2^{-80}$, recovering the secret key with $2^{29.50}$ decryption queries.

item.title: Registered Hierarchy-Based Signatures from Bilinear Groups
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2934
Authors: Jiamian Yan, Hong Yang, Ziyan Yuan, Borui Chen, Liang Zhang, Haibin Kan
Summary: Registration-based signatures (RBS) remove the trusted key generation center (KGC) of identity-based signatures, resolving the global key escrow problem: users generate their own secret state and publish public registration material, which a curator holding no cryptographic secrets aggregates into compact public parameters. Yet many scenarios need both registration to avoid key escrow across organizations and delegation for trust control within an organization. Delegated Reg-FE (ASIACRYPT'2025) realizes this hybrid trust model for encryption, but only for $2$-level hierarchies.
In this work, we introduce registered hierarchy-based signatures (RHBS), which combines registration of root users with hierarchical delegation to non-root users in $L$-level hierarchies. We construct RHBS from BBG-based hierarchical signatures using three techniques: cross-term cancellation to remove the KGC, plus affine share compression and power-of-two groups with version tag to obtain the properties below.
Our construction satisfies standard compactness, efficiency, and unbounded registration. It further achieves extra compactness for the common reference string, each root user's public registration material, and signatures. It also supports non-root key updates without re-delegation and public signature updates without re-signing when new registrations change the public parameters. We prove selective-identity unforgeability under the computational asymmetric $(L+1)$-BDHE assumption in the random-oracle model, even if all other root users are malicious. We implement our construction and compare its computational and storage costs with related schemes.

item.title: Hardware/Software Co-Design of ML-DSA with Random Delay Insertion Against Correlation Power Analysis
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2933
Authors: Salvatore Coppa, Ettore Napoli
Summary: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) recently led to the standardization of the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA). Standard software implementations of ML-DSA on embedded devices are exposed to physical side-channel attacks, since the power consumption of the circuit depends on the processed secret data and allows key recovery via Correlation Power Analysis (CPA). In addition, protecting these implementations in software introduces large latency overheads. In this paper, the physical vulnerability of ML-DSA is considered focusing the study on embedded microcontroller and System-on-Chip (SoC) platforms. The computational cost of software countermeasures, validated via Test Vector Leakage Assessment (TVLA), is evaluated on both architectures. An Hardware/Software co-design implemented on a Zynq-7000 SoC is then proposed to overcome the software execution bottleneck. The vulnerable pointwise Montgomery multiplication is offloaded to an Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI4-Full) hardware accelerator that integrates a 16-bit Linear Feedback Shift Register (LFSR) for Random Delay Insertion (RDI), preventing CPA trace alignment. Experimental results demonstrate a 13.4× speedup over the software-protected SoC implementation. The proposed architecture reduces the protected signing latency to 42.80 ms, achieving an execution time close to the 40.64 ms of the unprotected software implementation, while the dynamic power dissipated by the hardware accelerator in the programmable logic is limited to 33 mW.

item.title: Karu64: An Open RVA23 Processor with Vector Keccak Support
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2932
Authors: Markku-Juhani O. Saarinen, Thomas Szymkowiak
Summary: Can a whole-permutation Keccak instruction provide useful post-quantum acceleration inside a general-purpose vector application processor, despite its 1600-bit state and limited register-file bandwidth? We present, to our knowledge, the first hardware implementation of the standards-track RISC-V Zvknhk Vector Keccak extension. We integrate it alongside other vector cryptography support into Karu64, a new open-source application processor supporting the RVA23S64 profile. The complete system boots Debian Linux on a VCU118 FPGA at 75 MHz, allowing realistic OpenSSL benchmarking. Architecturally, the vkeccak.vi instruction gathers the state once, performs the permutation, and returns it through existing vector registers. This gives it excellent performance and allows usage from unmodified Linux userspace. In ideal-memory RTL simulation, resident-state SHAKE128/256 absorption and squeezing are $79$ - $83\times$ and $105$ - $116\times$ faster, respectively, than Clang-generated vector-enabled C with Zbb and Zvbb extensions. FPGA measurements under Linux show end-to-end ML-KEM and ML-DSA operations gain $1.48\times$ and $1.65\times$, respectively, over hand-vectorized implementations, due to the central role of Keccak in these PQC standards. A NanGate45 synthesis comparison shows a 2.29 % core-area increment over the implemented ratified-crypto baseline. These results establish practical feasibility of the fixed-group instruction, connecting standards-track semantics to integrated hardware cost and measured application benefit in a working Linux system.

item.title: Nonlinear invariants of CRAFT
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2931
Authors: Tim Beyne, Michiel Verbauwhede
Summary: This note shows that the round function of CRAFT admits nonlinear invariants that activate only four S-boxes. These invariants extend to invariants of the full cipher that hold for $2^{120}$ out of $2^{128}$ keys and $2^{60}$ out of $2^{64}$ possible tweaks. Since there are four similar nonlinear invariants that hold under independent conditions on the master key, this yields nearly $2^{122}$ weak keys for the all-zero tweak. If 64 different weak tweaks can be chosen, then for at least half of the keys, one or more of these nonlinear invariants holds. Further invariants with a slightly different structure can also be found. The same invariants were found independently by Roberto Civino. These results imply that CRAFT is, for all practical purposes, insecure.

item.title: BEEP: IOPPs from List Decoding with Better Elimination of Pretenders
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2930
Authors: Remco Bloemen, Albert Garreta
Summary: We present an improved soundness analysis of the DEEP technique for linear codes (after a minor modification), which, unlike its predecessor, results in negligible error bounds for parameters typically used in practice. The modification consists simply in performing $m$ DEEP samples, instead of one. The resulting DEEP sampling error decreases exponentially with $m$, and in practice $m=2$-$5$ makes it tiny. The subsequent folding error is of $(\delta \cdot n +1)/|\mathbb{F}|$, for $\delta$ a proximity parameter and $n$ the code length.
We modify typical code-based IOPPs with this technique, such as WHIR, Ligerito, Basefold, etc. As a result, we obtain code-based IOPPs that only require list decodability of the underlying codes, instead of Mutual Correlated Agreement (MCA), with smaller soundness errors than their counterparts.
Since it does not rely on MCA for its soundness, this improved DEEP technique allows to use arbitrary linear codes in IOPPs with $\delta$ up to the Johnson bound. Additionally, this opens the door to using codes (e.g. perhaps Reed-Solomon codes) with $\delta$ beyond the Johnson bound, assuming the code is $\delta$-list decodable, even if it does not have the $\delta$-MCA property.
Finally, we also provide an affine version of our improved DEEP analysis, where the folding challenges are affine polynomials instead of field elements, following [FS26,CWYZ26]. We provide a simple proof showing that, after the DEEP samples are done, the folding error with affine folding challenges is $2/|\mathbb{F}|$, which is smaller than the affine-MCA error from CWYZ26.

item.title: When Confirmation Tags Are Not Enough: Full Key Recovery from Ordinary Decapsulation Outputs in a HCR-KEM
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2929
Authors: Rafik HAMZA
Summary: Reconciliation in lattice-based key encapsulation mechanisms enables two parties to derive a common secret despite the presence of noise. However, confirming the reconciled value does not necessarily guarantee the validity of the ciphertext from which it was derived. In this paper, we investigate this security distinction through HCR-KEM, a reconciliation-based research construction that combines multi-shift forest reconciliation, an NTT-activity filter, a SHA3-256 confirmation tag, and implicit rejection.
We demonstrate a complete key-recovery attack using only ordinary 32-byte decapsulation outputs, without requiring an explicit validity oracle. By constructing source-admissible unit-monomial ciphertexts, we isolate individual signed relations while fixing 289 non-target reconciliation positions. We then exploit the resulting relations through a publicly verifiable signed-graph certificate to recover all 1,536 secret coefficients. To improve the efficiency of this recovery, we introduce graph-aware peeling, which uses previously recovered coefficients to reduce the complexity of subsequent binary recovery trees.
We evaluate the attack using the reference C implementation on 50 fresh matched keys. All 150 recovery executions succeed, with 3,000 correct honest-key predictions and no false matches among 3,000 negative controls. Graph-aware peeling requires an average of 3,565.18 decapsulation calls, compared with 4,382.54 for the optimal depth-four per-scalar method and 6,127.38 for the original method. This represents an 18.65\% reduction over the scalar-optimal baseline, with a mean paired saving of 817.36 calls and an approximate 95\% confidence interval of 810.49–824.23 calls.
Finally, we establish a conditional reconciliation-independence criterion and apply it to the guaranteed-rejection branch of standard ML-KEM. Our findings identify a concrete limitation of confirmation-only ciphertext validation and demonstrate how graph structure can be exploited to improve adaptive key recovery.

item.title: Shifting Dark Matter: Two-Query Key Recovery on a Post-Quantum OPRF
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2928
Authors: Hanbeom Shin, Insung Kim, Seokhie Hong, Dongjae Lee
Summary: At the 2026 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, Aranha et al. proposed a maliciously secure post-quantum oblivious pseudorandom function (OPRF) from Crypto Dark Matter. Its strong PRF is $F_k(x) = B \cdot \mathrm{vec}(k \cdot \mathrm{elt}(E(x))) \bmod 3$, where the key $k \in \mathbb{F}_{2^n}$ multiplies a systematic encoding $E(x)$. In this paper, we show that a client that follows the protocol recovers the key from two chosen queries. Multiplication by $\alpha^{-2}$ commutes with the key multiplication and acts on the polynomial basis as a shift, up to a correction from two bits. We prove that input pairs whose encodings differ by the factor $\alpha^2$ correspond to the binary solutions of six linear systems over $\mathbb{F}_3$. For the proposed parameters, we found such a pair in 146 seconds. After a guess of two bits, the outputs give a full-weight ternary syndrome decoding instance whose 164 equations almost always determine the other 254 bits of $k \cdot \mathrm{elt}(E(x))$. Counting memory in list elements, we estimate time and memory complexities of $2^{67.3}$ and $2^{51.8}$, or $2^{69.9}$ and $2^{33.3}$, both far below the claimed 128-bit security. For a 64-bit security target, the whole attack recovered the key with $2^{34.39}$ operations, matching our cost model. A dense field modulus does not prevent the attack. For 128-bit inputs, a non-systematic code of length at least 160 heuristically removes such pairs, and a public $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear mixing of the output removes the linear structure of the key recovery.

item.title: On the Hardness of LWE with Trapdoor Hints and Applications to Fuzzy Cryptography
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2927
Authors: Divesh Aggarwal, Aayush Jain, Huijia Lin, Yuetian Wu
Summary: Learning with Errors (LWE) and its variants have revolutionized modern cryptography, enabling a wide range of applications that previously seemed out of reach. In recent years, there has been growing interest in hinted variants of LWE, in which the adversary receives carefully structured side information, and these assumptions have further expanded the cryptographic toolkit. In this work, we study a natural hinted LWE assumption that we call LWE with Trapdoor Hints. Concretely, we consider the hardness of distinguishing an LWE sample $(\mathbf{A},\, \mathbf{s}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{e}^{\mathsf{T}} \bmod q)$ from uniform even in the presence of a full-rank homogeneous trapdoor $\mathbf{T}$ for $\mathbf{A}$. We show that when the error $\mathbf{e}$ is drawn from a Gaussian distribution that is only slightly wider than the decoding radius associated with $\mathbf{T}$, this problem remains hard under the standard LWE assumption. We then present two compelling applications of this problem that were previously out of reach:
First, we construct the first Euclidean-ball obfuscator from LWE satisfying distributional virtual black-box security. Our construction achieves the functional preserving property, reusability, and distributional VBB security, assuming the obfuscated inputs are drawn from a suitable LWE-compatible distribution such as a discrete Gaussian. To the best of our knowledge, such a notion was not previously known even assuming indistinguishability obfuscation. As a byproduct, we resolve the open question posed by Fuller, Meng, and Reyzin (Asiacrypt 2013) concerning using lattice trapdoors to construct computational fuzzy extractors supporting the Euclidean metric and with drastically larger error tolerance.
Second, we introduce a new primitive that we call Threshold Difference Revealing Encryption (TDRE), which can be viewed as a public-key, two-input analogue of fuzzy extractors. Standard fuzzy extractors are highly effective for fuzzy authentication, but they are fundamentally asymmetric and do not directly support the task of comparing two independently encoded, hidden biometrics. We believe that TDRE can help fill this important conceptual gap in current techniques for fuzzy cryptography.

item.title: γ₁₁: Computational Certificates — the macadamias 0001, 0014, 0015, 0059 and 0052
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2926
Authors: Rémi Géraud-Stewart, David Naccache
Summary: The macadamias are the ten perfect forms of rank 9 for which the proof of the Hermite constant $\gamma_{11}$ cannot be completed at rank 10. Four of them, 0001, 0014, 0059 and 0015, were treated at rank 11 by contact geometry in our previous work, and a fifth, 0052, by a gluing argument with a computer proof. To reduce dependency on pen-and-paper mathematical proofs and increase confidence in the announced results, this paper gives a second, machine-checked confirmation of these five cases. The new proof relies on computed certificates. A certificate counts only in general mode: it must hold for every lattice of rank nine that is admissibly marked by the form, and not only for the form itself. The certificate of a form is a tree of boxes over the space of its first gluings, every leaf of which is checked exactly, together with a ball of gluings around the rank-ten lattice stored with the form, on which some leaves rely. The ball comes from an exact theorem in which the gluing and the rank-nine member both move; the bound $\det L\ge 972$ follows from the inequality $\det L\ge\det M\,(4-\rho^2(M))$ between a lattice $L$ of rank 11, its primitive sublattice $M$ of rank 10 and the covering radius $\rho(M)$. For 0059 the ball uses a contact-cone certificate of degree three; for 0015, whose stored lattice has no margin, a sharper localisation and an off-mean covering bound, both proved here; 0052 needs no ball. We state what each program checks, give the checking algorithms, all in integer and rational arithmetic, including a parallel final verification of a tree, and describe the publicly available database that stores the certificates, with the commands that check each form again from the database, the build and the reproduction pack. Floating point is used to find certificates but never to accept them. The five certificates check again, by a second route, the proofs of these five cases in our previous papers; they do not replace them.

item.title: A Quasipolynomial Quantum Algorithm for the Vector Dihedral Coset Problem with Smooth Modulus
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2925
Authors: Aparna Gupte
Summary: We give a quantum algorithm for the vector dihedral coset problem over $\mathbb{Z}_q^n$, in which the goal is to recover $\mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{Z}_q^n$ given independent samples of the form $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bigl(\ket{0,\mathbf{x}}+\ket{1,\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{s}}\bigr)$, for $\mathbf{x}\sim \mathbb{Z}_q^n$. When the modulus $q$ is $B$-smooth, the algorithm uses $n^{O(B^{1+o(1)}\log q)}B^{O(B^{2+o(1)}\log q)}$ samples and time. For $B = \mathrm{polylog}(n)$ and $q=\mathrm{poly}(n)$, this gives a quasipolynomial time- and sample-complexity. This extends the previously known quasipolynomial-time result for power-of-two moduli (Bonnetain, Naya-Plasencia, ASIACRYPT 2018; Bai, Jangir, Kirshanova, Ngo, Youmans, CRYPTO 2025).
The algorithm proceeds by reducing the modulus one prime factor $p | q$ at a time. The key ingredient is a sieving procedure that clears the non-linear terms in the phase modulo $p$ via an algorithm of Ivanyos and Santha (TCS 2017) that finds non-zero $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{F}_p^\ell$ such that $\sum_{i \in [\ell]} u_i^d \mathbf{a}_i = 0 \mod p$ for degrees $1 \le d \le p-1$, given vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_\ell \in \mathbb{F}_p^n$ as input.
The algorithm also applies to the extrapolated dihedral coset problem (EDCP) introduced by Brakerski, Kirshanova, Stehlé, and Wen (PKC 2018), which is known to be equivalent to LWE in the polynomial sample regime. However, our result does not yield a new attack on LWE in any regime, precisely because the known reduction from LWE to EDCP provides only polynomially many clean samples, whereas our algorithm requires quasipolynomially many samples.
The main algorithm was obtained in a GPT-5.6 Sol conversation prompted by the author; the author is responsible for all statements, proofs, and correctness. Concurrent work of Boucher, Fouque, and Shen gives an algorithm with similar guarantees for prime-power moduli.

item.title: The Swell Protocol: Invite-Bound Hybrid Key Agreement, a Double Ratchet with an ML-KEM Epoch Ratchet, and a Signed Server Statement
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2924
Authors: Ilyas Akbar Almadani
Summary: We describe the Swell Protocol, the end-to-end encryption protocol of the Swell messenger, as fixed by draft 3 of its specification. First contact uses an out-of-band invite code instead of a server-held prekey directory: a hybrid X25519/ML-KEM-768 handshake in the style of PQXDH, without prekey signatures, whose transcript is bound to the invite. Sessions then run the Double Ratchet with header encryption, extended by a post-quantum epoch ratchet: ML-KEM-768 exchanges carried inside the conversation renew an epoch key that is mixed into every message key, so that after a one-time state compromise confidentiality is restored against an adversary who is passive while healing, even if it later breaks every X25519 key. Sessions between existing contacts are started or repaired by link frames sealed under a static-static key. Groups fan out over pairwise sessions with identity-signed group states. Separately, the message relay publishes an hourly statement signed under a pinned key and kept in a hash-chained, append-only log meant to be mirrored by an external witness. We state the threat model precisely, including two admitted limits of forward secrecy, and we report symbolic analyses in ProVerif and Tamarin of simplified models, together with every attack those models found; there is no computational proof. The protocol has had internal review only; it has not undergone an independent security audit. We list the open problems and invite cryptanalysis.

item.title: Early-Stopping Dishonest Majority Broadcast with Linear Rounds and Polynomial Communication
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2923
Authors: Renas Bacho, Kecheng Shi
Summary: Early-stopping Byzantine broadcast protocols adapt their round complexity to the number $f\le t$ of parties that are actually corrupted in an execution, where $t<n$, all honest parties output and terminate within $O(f+1)$ rounds, using polynomial communication and computation. This matches the classical early-stopping lower bound of $\min\{f+2,t+1\}$ rounds up to a constant factor. Our basic protocol terminates within $14f+9$ rounds and communicates $O(\kappa n^7)$ bits, where $\kappa$ is the length of a signature. Two optimized variants improve both bounds: the first terminates within $5f+2\lceil\log_2(f+1)\rceil+10$ rounds and communicates $O(\kappa n^5)$ bits, and the second terminates within $5f+2\lfloor\sqrt f\rfloor+11$ rounds and communicates $O(\kappa n^4+n^{9/2})$ bits.

item.title: PC-DGS: A Pool-Certified Dynamic Group Signature Scheme Based on XMSS
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2922
Authors: Qiyan Sang, Lin Zhou, Huiyan Chen
Summary: Hash-based group signatures provide a conservative approach to post-quantum anonymous authentication, but existing constructions often face a tension between stateless signing, compact signatures, and dynamic group management. This paper proposes PC-DGS, a pool-certified dynamic group signature scheme based on XMSS-certified WOTS+ one-time credentials. The main idea is to separate offline credential certification from online message signing: the group administrator uses XMSS to certify user-generated WOTS+ public keys, while users later sign messages using lightweight one-time WOTS+ credentials. This yields a signer-side stateful but public-verifier stateless design, reducing the communication overhead inherited from SPHINCS+-style constructions. To mitigate batch-level linkability, PC-DGS introduces a shuffled index-pool mechanism for randomized XMSS leaf allocation. To prevent malicious-administrator framing, each user registers a Merkle authorization root that binds the administrator to a pre-authorized set of user-generated WOTS+ public keys. We analyze PC-DGS under standard hash-based and authenticated-encryption assumptions and establish public-verifier anonymity, traceability, non-frameability, revocation correctness, credential-reuse detectability, and signer-side forward security for used credentials. Parameterized evaluation shows that PC-DGS achieves low-kilobyte signatures, with representative profiles ranging from about 1.5 KB to 5.4 KB.

item.title: CKKS Acceleration for Next-Wave Homomorphic Encryption
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2921
Authors: Xuan Wang, Sanjay Deshpande, Jaehyung Kim, Jakub Szefer, Tajana Rosing, Patrick Longa
Summary: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) is a powerful cryptographic tool that enables computation directly on encrypted data without first decrypting it. It allows privacy-preserving computing where sensitive data is processed in the cloud or in other untrusted environments. Emerging functional bootstrapping and coefficient-based matrix-multiplication techniques offer opportunities to accelerate nonlinear and linear computations, respectively. However, there is still a gap between their theoretical advantages and achievable hardware performance gains. We present GEAR, an algorithm–architecture co-design for efficient FHE acceleration supporting recent CKKS advancements while preserving full conventional CKKS functionality for existing workloads. On the algorithmic side, we propose FusedFBS, a fused functional bootstrapping algorithm that combines coefficient-based matrix multiplication with grafting-enabled functional bootstrapping to enable high-precision, hardware-friendly FHE computation. On the hardware side, we propose the GEAR architecture, with a Modular Systolic Array and a Mixed-Radix Constant-Geometry NTT Unit, to accelerate key kernels. These mechanisms balance efficient execution with flexibility for evolving FHE algorithms, making it a versatile FHE accelerator. We demonstrate FusedFBS through encrypted Deep Learning inference. Across representative workloads, GEAR achieves more than 3000$\times$ speedup over the CPU baseline. Compared with state-of-the-art CKKS accelerators, it delivers significant speedup under similar area and power budgets.

item.title: Processor-Aware Quantum Time-Memory-Data Trade-Offs
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2920
Authors: Aniket Ghara, Suman Pal, Prokash Kumar Kundu, Arpita Maitra
Summary: Time--memory--data trade-offs (TMDTOs) provide a fundamental framework for cryptanalytic attacks that balance preprocessing,memory, online computation, and available target data. In the quantum setting, Dunkelman et al. introduced quantum TMDTO attacks based on GroverMatch, obtaining the relation $N^2=T^{4/3}M^2D^2$ for multiple-target inversion using a single quantum processor. In this work, we introduce a processor-aware formulation of quantum TMDTOs by incorporating parallel quantum computation into the GroverMatch framework. We partition the flavour space across $K$ parallel quantum processors and use quantum counting to identify a promising local subspace, followed by Grover search within that subspace. Under an idealized parallel wall-clock model, we show that the online complexity becomes $ T_K = \frac{t^{3/2}}{\sqrt{K}} $, and consequently derive the processor-aware trade-off $ N^2 = T_K^{4/3}M^2D^2K^{2/3} $. The relation specializes to the previously known single-processor quantum TMDTO relation when $K=1$. We instantiate the framework for both Quantum Hellman and Quantum Rainbow constructions and show that, for fixed $N$, $M$, and $D$, parallelization reduces the online wall-clock time by a factor $\sqrt{K}$, at the cost of increasing the aggregate quantum work by a factor of $\sqrt{K}$. We further analyze the resulting trade-off against generic Grover search under both single-processor and equal-processor-budget comparisons. Our results provide a processor-aware characterization of quantum TMDTO attacks and clarify the trade-off between quantum hardware parallelism and online cryptanalytic time.

item.title: Adaptively Secure Batched IBE from LWE
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2919
Authors: Jiaqi Cheng, Pratish Datta
Summary: We construct the first adaptively secure (epoch-based) batched identity-based encryption (BIBE) scheme from the learning with errors (LWE) assumption in the plain model. In addition to achieving adaptive security, we obtain significant efficiency improvements over existing lattice-based constructions. The public parameters, batch keys, and ciphertexts have sizes independent of the batch size, and setup requires no prescribed batch-size bound, unlike other lattice-based constructions. The authority generates batch keys from short, publicly computable digests. Encryption time is independent of the batch size, while decrypting an entire batch takes time linear in its size, including public preprocessing.
We first give a plain-model generic construction from laconic function evaluation and tagged one-key functional encryption. Building on this generic construction, we then exploit the linear structure of laconic encryption to obtain a more efficient algebraic construction using tagged inner-product functional encryption. Using receiver non-committing encryption, we further obtain an adaptively secure variant in the random oracle model that avoids noise flooding in the laconic encryption component in our plain-model construction and permits a polynomial modulus-to-noise ratio for that component.
Finally, we give a generic transformation from BIBE to threshold BIBE using threshold fully homomorphic encryption. The transformation preserves adaptive security against static corruptions and requires only one round of communication for batch-key generation after a trusted setup.

item.title: Nonlinear Invariant Attacks on Full CRAFT: Chosen-Tweak Key Recovery
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2918
Authors: Roberto Civino
Summary: A nonlinear invariant is a Boolean function of the state that every round preserves, up to a constant, for a class of keys. It then relates plaintext and ciphertext with correlation one, whatever the number of rounds. Finding one is in general a problem about the whole state.
We study a family of invariants of the tweakable block cipher CRAFT for which this problem splits into independent pieces. Each function reads half of the state linearly and the other half through components of the S-box, one nibble at a time, so that the condition for a round to preserve it becomes one small condition per S-box, read once from the algebraic normal form of the S-box. The family can therefore be analysed by hand and enumerated by computer.
The simplest member uses a single quadratic component of the S-box and survives all thirty-two rounds on a class of $2^{108}$ keys. Allowing cubic components and a pattern that alternates between even and odd rounds yields an invariant that survives all thirty-two rounds for half of all keys, with suitably chosen tweaks. Both classes are determined exactly, and a computer classification shows that none in the family is larger. Since the conditions are periodic with the tweakey, these invariants pass any number of rounds, not only the thirty-two of CRAFT, so increasing the round count would not remove them.
The invariants give key recovery. Almost every key of CRAFT satisfies a great many of them at once, and the classification yields a library of hundreds of thousands. Running the library against an unknown key and collecting the linear relations each invariant reveals recovers, for essentially every key, an average of 61.3 of the 64 low key bits with about $2^{14.5}$ chosen-tweak queries and negligible time. Over a sample of 5000 random keys every one was broken, the remaining search staying below the 124-bit security claim in every case. All programs and data that reproduce these results are available in a public repository.

item.title: Six Passes Are Enough: Security Proofs for NIST AES Key Wrap
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2917
Authors: Yuwen Zhou
Summary: AES Key Wrap protects keys entering and leaving hardware security modules and keys exchanged through S/MIME, JOSE and PKCS#11. NIST standardized it as KW and KWP in SP 800-38F and is now revising that document. In twenty-five years the algorithm has received no security proof, and apart from a remark on very long messages, nothing published explains its six passes of AES. Its design breaks the assumptions of existing proofs in three ways. One AES key serves every step, whereas proofs for generalized Feistel networks assume independent round functions; the chaining value has only 64 bits, so collisions on it occur long before the birthday bound of AES and a proof cannot exclude them; and unwrapping runs the algorithm backward on adversarial ciphertexts, which the usual arguments handle only with independently keyed halves. We prove that if AES is a strong pseudorandom permutation (PRP), the six-pass wrapping function at the core of the standard is also a strong PRP, with main term $88\,\sigma^2/2^{128}$ for $\sigma$ semiblocks of data. KW and KWP are deterministic authenticated encryption schemes, with an additional term for guessing the 64-bit check value.
