Our main step is to sample the intermediate values of each message from both ends, forward from the input and backward from the output, and to join the two sides in the middle, which treats forward and inverse queries alike. Every bad event then involves at most two messages and needs two independent 64-bit collisions, which we count rather than exclude. The count needs only two passes on each side of the join and one for the join, so five passes give a bound of the same form and the sixth is to spare. Two passes, by contrast, can be distinguished from random with $2^{32}$ short queries. All bounds extend to many independent keys without a loss in the number of keys.

item.title: Cleve's Bound Is Tight: Optimally Fair Coin Flipping for Every Fixed Number of Parties
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2916
Authors: Yuwen Zhou
Summary: Proof-of-stake chains, committee selection and lotteries draw public randomness from protocols whose participants may collude. Cleve [STOC 1986] showed that without an honest majority, aborting alone lets a coalition bias the outcome of any $r$-round $n$-party coin flip by $\Omega(1/r)$. Moran, Naor and Segev [TCC 2009] matched this bound for two parties, and later work came within a $\sqrt{\log r}$ factor of it for three. For four or more parties, the best known bias is about $r^{-1/2-1/(2^{n-1}-2)}$, which approaches the $r^{-1/2}$ of the simple majority protocol as $n$ grows. The obstacle is recovery: after an abort, the remaining parties must carry on without giving the coalition a fresh chance to bias the outcome. In the best earlier protocol they reconstruct a noisy copy of the current expected outcome, and with more than three parties this costs a power of $r$ at each level. We show that Cleve's bound is tight for every fixed number of parties. Assuming constant-round oblivious transfer and constant-round passively secure computation, we give an $n$-party $r$-round protocol over a broadcast channel whose bias against $n-1$ corrupted parties is $O(n^3 2^n / r)$. The protocol draws the outcome at the start and keeps it secret, and the coins it reveals form a random walk conditioned on that outcome. After an abort, the remaining parties reconstruct nothing: they start a new run whose outcome probability is a public table evaluated on bits they hold in secret-shared form. Our main technical result is that the entries of every such table stay within a factor of two of each other, however many aborts came before, so each level of recovery costs only a constant factor. The protocol therefore improves on majority for up to about $\frac{1}{2}\log_2 r$ parties, and a variant for any number of parties has an exponential factor set only by how many more parties are corrupted than honest.

item.title: A New Cryptanalytic Attack on an RSA Variant Arising from Cubic Pell Curves
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2915
Authors: Brahim Chnioune, Mohammed Rahmani, Abderrahmane Nitaj, Mhammed Ziane
Summary: In 2024, Nitaj and Seck introduced an RSA-like cryptosystem defined by a public key $(N,e)$ and a corresponding private key $(N,d)$ satisfying $ ed-1 \equiv 0 \pmod{p^{2(a-1)} q^{2(b-1)} (p-1)^2 (q-1)^2}, $ where $N=p^aq^b.$ More recently, Seck and Tchapgnouo (DAM 2026) proposed a partial key exposure attack against the same scheme for the case where $N = pq$, assuming partial knowledge of one prime factor. Using a lattice-based method, they showed that, under some constraints, the private parameters $(d,p,q)$ can be recovered in polynomial time. In this paper, we further investigate the security of this construction by considering a dual-key scenario. Specifically, in the presence of two encryption exponents $e_1$ and $e_2$, with corresponding private exponents $d_1$ and $d_2$ satisfying $ e_i d_i - 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{(p-1)^2(q-1)^2}, $ for $i \in \{1,2\}$, we prove that if the prime factors of $N$ share a certain number of least significant bits, and if $d_1$ and $d_2$ share an amount of their most significant bits, then the private parameters $(d_1,d_2,p,q)$ can be computed in polynomial time. Our method combines an extension of Coppersmith's small-root technique with lattice basis reduction, leading to improved bounds compared to existing single-key attacks.

item.title: Recovering HQC Secret Key from Distance Spectrum using Side-Channel Attack
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2914
Authors: Magali Salom, Angélique Lopez, Valentin Vasseur, Gabriel Zaid
Summary: HQC is a code-based key encapsulation mechanism selected for standardiza- tion by NIST. It uses sparse secret vectors in a quasi-cyclic structure, where GJS-style attacks can exploit correlations between private syndrome weight and the secret-key distance spectrum. However, HQC decapsulation does not directly manipulate any syndrome, leaving open whether any such attack could be performed in practice. In this work, we present the first practical end-to-end side-channel attack against HQC that recovers the secret key through error-weight leakage and distance-spectrum reconstruction. We identify two sources of leakage in the Reed–Muller decoder under different attacker capabilities. In a chosen-ciphertext attack (CCA), we exploit the ExpandAndSum function by imposing a zero message, whereas in a known-ciphertext attack (KCA), we target the FindPeaks function without modifying the legitimate encapsulation procedure. We provide a theoretical characterization of the Hadamard coefficients manipulated by FindPeaks, establishing a direct relationship between the highest peak and the error weight under a sufficient decoding condition, while showing that the remaining coefficients also depend on the error pattern. We develop profiled side-channel attacks to estimate the error weight and construct a soft distance spectrum of the secret key. To recover the key from imperfect in- formation, we introduce a simulated-annealing reconstruction algorithm that, in simulations, reduces the number of required error-weight observations by approxi- mately 5.8× compared with the state-of-the-art SSV26 method, with substantially lower reconstruction times. Our experiments on an ARM Cortex-M4 implementation of HQC-1 demonstrate end-to-end secret-key recovery in both attack settings. In the CCA setting, our algorithm achieves a 93.5% success rate with 40 000 decapsulation traces, compared to 200 000 traces for SSV26, and recovers the secret key in all 200 trials with 100 000 traces. Most notably, in the more restrictive KCA setting, our approach recovers the secret key in all 200 trials using 1 000 000 traces, whereas the reconstruction algorithm from SSV26 fails to recover the key in any of the 200 trials, even with 1 300 000 traces.

item.title: A Collision for 38-Step SHA-256
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2913
Authors: Omer Goldzweig
Summary: We give a collision for 38-step SHA-256 from the standard initial value, to our knowledge the first. The attack is a two-block differential attack whose message differences are in the same words as in the 38-step semi-free-start collision of Mendel, Nad and Schläffer. Most state words of the second block are fixed in advance. For each first block, a table indexed by the first word of the chaining value supplies the first state words, and one lookup on a 32-bit key matches them with the last free state words so that the characteristic holds through step 17; the remaining steps hold by chance. The expected time is $2^{54.8}$ calls of the 38-step compression function, with $2^{57.5}$ table accesses that this count does not charge. The tables take 7.4 GB, and finding the fixed state words took 52,300 vCPU-hours. A search of 53 GPU-hours found the collision after about 10% of the expected work.

item.title: Intergalactic Consensus: Asynchronous Bitcoin Clients
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2912
Authors: Odysseas Sofikitis, Dionysis Zindros
Summary: Bitcoin is a synchronous proof of work consensus protocol. Its security against a minority adversary rests on the synchrony among the validators, and that assumption is known to be necessary. Bitcoin clients have inherited it: every client construction to date assumes that messages arrive on time and that at least one of its peers is honest. We show that a client needs neither. We keep the validators synchronous and give the client an asynchronous connection to them, over which the adversary may delay or drop any message and may herself answer. The client holds a clock and nothing else. Bitcoin confirms a block once it is $k$ blocks deep in the chain, for a constant $k$. Our client confirms a block once it is deep enough for the current round and for the height of the chain it received. We prove the rule safe and live in the bitcoin backbone model: the client confirms a prefix of every honest chain, and the confirmed prefix grows at a constant rate. Asynchrony costs latency. A client that receives an honest chain at round $r$ discards a $\rho^2$ fraction of it, where $\rho$ bounds the mining power of the adversary relative to the honest validators. It discards $\Theta(r)$ blocks where a synchronous client discards a constant, and it confirms a block $\Theta(r)$ rounds after the honest validators do. We prove this tight: against a private mining adversary, every safe rule that reads only the round and the height discards asymptotically as much, and no constant depth is safe.

item.title: FL$^{2}$RS: Forward-Secure Lattice-based Linkable Ring Signature for Vehicle Anonymity in VANETs
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2911
Authors: Junjie Bian, Dong Xie, Ningning Dong, Fulong Chen, Weixin Bian, Taochun Wang
Summary: Ring signatures have been extensively researched for Vehicular Ad Hoc Network communications, aiming to safeguard vehicles’ identity privacy and the authenticity of traffic messages. While a variety of such schemes have emerged in recent years, the overwhelming majority still depend on classical hardness assumptions, such as the difficulty of discrete logarithms or integer factorization, which are precisely the problems that quantum computing threatens to resolve efficiently. Moreover, forward security, as a critical cryptographic property, has not been adequately addressed or implemented in existing quantum-resistant schemes. In this paper, we introduce FL$^{2}$RS, a novel linkable ring signature built on lattice assumptions with forward security for VANETs to ensure vehicle privacy through anonymity and enable linkability detection of multiple signatures from the same vehicle. Moreover, forward-secure unforgeability guarantees the security of previous ring signatures even if an adversary obtains the signer's current secret key. To achieve this, we adopt a ternary tree structure to divide epochs and leverage lattice basis algorithms to enable one-way key evolution, so that vehicles refresh their secret keys at regular intervals. We conduct a thorough security analysis and compare our scheme with prior works. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that FL$^{2}$RS offers the best verifying efficiency, competitive signing and communication performance.

item.title: Automatic Preimage Attacks on Xoodyak Based on Linear Structures
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2910
Authors: Zhaoyue Huang, Meicheng Liu, Dongdai Lin
Summary: Xoodyak was one of the ten finalists in the NIST Lightweight Cryptography standardization process (2018-2023). In this paper, we investigate preimage attacks on Xoodyak-XOF using linear structures with the allocation model. A key challenge in applying this approach is to identify suitable linear structures that lead to efficient preimage attacks. To address this challenge, we propose an automatic framework for searching suitable linear structures. The framework incorporates three techniques: a mixed exact and linear approximation of the $\chi$ function in the final round, a mixed integer linear programming model for describing the propagation of linear variables through the $\chi$ and XOR functions, and weighted condition constraints with a weight update algorithm to guide the structure search. Based on the linear structures identified by the proposed framework, we improve the preimage attacks on 2-round and 3-round Xoodyak-XOF with a 128-bit output, reducing their complexities to $2^{93.934}$ and $2^{115.715}$, respectively, which are the best known results to date. In addition, we present the first theoretical preimage attack on 4-round Xoodyak-XOF, with a complexity of $2^{126.245}$.

item.title: Kairos: Efficient High-Threshold Asynchronous Distributed Key Generation from Lightweight Cryptography
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2909
Authors: Xinxin Xing, Yizhong Liu, Zifan Li, Jianwei Liu, Yudi Yang, Yuan Lu, Song Bian, Zhenyu Guan, Tianwei Zhang
Summary: Asynchronous distributed key generation (ADKG) bootstraps threshold cryptosystems by robustly generating threshold public and private key pairs. This primitive is a fundamental building block for distributed algorithms such as random beacons, threshold signatures, threshold decryption, and general distributed key management services (DKM). While significant progress has been made, ADKG constructions still exhibit computation inefficiency, especially in high-threshold reconstruction, due to their tight coupling to homomorphic-commitment-based verifiable secret sharing.
We fill in this research gap by presenting Kairos, a concretely and asymptotically efficient ADKG protocol. For efficiency, Kairos avoids homomorphic commitments by deriving dLog-based public-private key sharings from the lightweight hash-based asynchronous complete secret sharing (ACSS), with an asymptotically optimal, quadratic per-key communication. For secrecy, Kairos tolerates up to $f$ malicious nodes among $n=3f+1$ parties, and produces unbiased public key shares with a high reconstruction threshold of $t\geq f$. The core techniques in Kairos are a non-interactive threshold lifting for private key shares, and a lightweight high-threshold verification script aggregator for public key shares under a lock-then-verify paradigm, which may be of independent interest and applied in asynchronous dynamic proactive secret sharing (ADPSS) or multi-party computation. Evaluations conducted on distributed AWS EC2 servers demonstrate that Kairos reduces 63.7-99.4\% runtime compared to the baselines DXKR23 (Usenix Security'23) and HARTS (ASIACRYPT'24) under $t=2f$, achieving a throughput of 3k keys/min at $n=16$. When applied in ADPSS, our solution reduces 91.0-98.7\% runtime compared to LongLive (Usenix Security'23) at $t=2f$, resharing 2.3k secrets/min across 16-node committees.

item.title: From Decoding Leakage to Full Key Recovery: A Single-Trace Attack on FALCON
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2908
Authors: Merve Karabulut, Panasayya Yalla, Reza Azarderakhsh, Mehran Mozaffari Kermani
Summary: FALCON is one of the post-quantum signature schemes selected by NIST. Its compact keys make it attractive for embedded devices, which are exposed to side-channel attacks. Such attacks on FALCON have so far targeted its Gaussian sampler, its floating-point arithmetic, and its number-theoretic transform. We instead attack a step that runs before any of these and has gone unexamined: the routine that decodes the secret key at the start of every signing. We show that this decoding leaks each secret coefficient through two intermediate values it forms. One arises in the decoding itself, the other in the modular conversion that follows. A profiled template attack on these two points recovers each coefficient of the secret polynomials from a single power trace with $98.32\%$ accuracy. Each prediction also carries a confidence score. A single trace does not recover every coefficient, so we add a key-recovery step. It ranks the predictions by confidence and solves the public key relation $g = h\cdot f$ for the rest, using only linear algebra and no lattice reduction. We evaluate the attack on an off-the-shelf ARM Cortex-M4 running FALCON-1024 at its nominal clock. The attack recovers the complete secret key for all 1000 tested keys, requiring 11.04 seconds on average. The decoding routine is shared across FALCON implementations, and the countermeasures proposed for the sampler and the arithmetic do not cover it. It must therefore be protected before FALCON is deployed.

item.title: Sparse-zkVC: Sparsity-Aware R1CS Synthesis for Zero-Knowledge Proofs of Sparse LLM Inference
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2907
Authors: yanzhe cheng, Luxing Yang, Wei Ren
Summary: Zero-knowledge proofs for machine-learning inference are often limited by dense arithmetization: even after model pruning, R1CS generators may instantiate witness variables and linear-combination terms according to the original tensor shape. Sparse-zkVC extends zkVC's CRPC+PSQ matrix-multiplication generator with mask-guided synthesis. Given a public static pruning mask, it allocates variables only for retained weights and active prefix-sum states while advancing CRPC coefficients over the original dense index order. This preserves coefficient alignment, keeps the constraint count at the inner dimension $d$, and reduces the dominant variable term from $h d m$ to $h\cdot NNZ$, where $NNZ$ counts retained weights. The prototype removes unused variables and linear-combination terms during frontend synthesis. On the zkVC-aligned $128\times64\times49$ benchmark, 99\% sparsity reduces variables from 412,736 to 12,191 and improves online proving time by 20.2$\times$, with all generated proofs verifying successfully. Long-context and LLaMA-7B linear-operator stress tests characterize the resulting efficiency gains and remaining single-node memory limits.

item.title: Improving the Efficiency of 4-Dimensional SQIsign
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2906
Authors: Dustin Ray, Paulo L. Barreto
Summary: SQIsignHD verifies a dimension-4 isogeny where SQIsign verifies a dimension-2 one, which removes the auxiliary curve from the signature but makes verification much costlier. We show that the verifier's chain of dimension-4 isogenies respects an automorphism of order 4 that acts on its theta coordinates as one fixed permutation, for every input, honest or forged. After the gluing, two of the four kernel points can therefore be recovered from the other two by permuting coordinates, and the constants of each step are determined by ten coordinates instead of sixteen, which cuts the verifier's cost by 37 to 40%. Along the way we derive the change of basis that the verifier applies at the gluing, which Dartois states with only a brief justification, prove that the verifier's image check remains sound with the signs that its implementation leaves free, and show that the verifier must validate the basis hints, which a forger controls. We implement the scheme at the round-3 SQIsign primes, adopted after Wesolowski's attack. At level I a signature takes 139 bytes, against 200 for the round-3 specification, and key and signature together take 223 bytes, the smallest level-I combination of any post-quantum signature we are aware of at parameters that stand after that attack; verification costs 4.3 times that of the dimension-2 scheme in the same code.

item.title: TRAVESS: Traceable Threshold VSS with Publicly Verifiable Shares and Tracing Evidence
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2905
Authors: Wenxing Duan, Huiran Zheng, Man Ho Au
Summary: Secret sharing protects a secret against coalitions below the reconstruction threshold, but it does not stop participants from selling their shares. Traceable secret sharing (TSS) holds participants accountable for such leakage: when a coalition packages its shares into a leaked program, called a reconstruction box, that recovers the secret given enough additional shares, a tracer can identify the traitors by querying this box on specially crafted artificial shares. Meanwhile, by allowing participants to verify that their shares are well-formed, verifiable secret sharing (VSS) addresses a different threat: a dishonest dealer distributing inconsistent shares. Boneh, Partap, and Rotem (CRYPTO 2024) posed the combination of TSS and VSS as an open problem, observing that share verification allows a reconstruction box to detect and reject the artificial shares used by their tracing procedures. We present TRAVESS, a threshold construction of traceable verifiable secret sharing. To our knowledge, it is the first construction to combine public share verification and reconstruction consistency with secrecy, tracer secrecy, non-imputability, and black-box traceability in the framework of Boneh et al. Our key idea is to use a trapdoor commitment scheme to enable the tracer to generate artificial shares that pass the same public verification as genuine shares. The tracer gains this capability without learning the secret, while the dealer remains bound to consistent shares. TRAVESS supports imperfect reconstruction boxes and produces evidence that anyone can verify using public information alone. We establish these guarantees in an ideal-functionality hybrid model.

item.title: Blind Deep-Learning Side-Channel Analysis of XTS-AES on a Commercial RISC-V Microcontroller
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2904
Authors: Keerthi Kamalakshan, Dirmanto Jap, Trevor Yap, Shivam Bhasin
Summary: The XTS-AES mode is widely deployed to provide storage encryption in embedded systems, where hardware accelerators are commonly used to protect sensitive firmware stored in external flash. Existing side-channel attacks against XTS-AES typically assume access to operation-level leakage, requiring precise segmentation of individual AES executions or exploiting implementation-specific temporal structures. Such assumptions are difficult to satisfy for commercial hardware accelerators, where cryptographic operations are tightly integrated and exposed only through coarse-grained leakage.
This paper presents a blind side-channel analysis methodology for hardware XTS-AES implementations that operates directly on complete power traces without requiring operation-level segmentation or knowledge of execution boundaries. The proposed approach adapted the blind deep learning-based side channel analysis to recover the XTS-AES encryption key from full-trace measurements. We further show that recovery of key can help to reconstruct the sector-specific XTS tweak, eliminating the need to recover the second XTS key.
The proposed methodology is evaluated on the hardware XTS-AES of a commercial ESP32-C3 microcontroller. Experimental results demonstrate successful recovery of the encryption key, reconstruction of the sector-specific tweak, and demonstrates how this can be used to recover the flash contents. The results highlight the practical feasibility of blind whole-trace side-channel analysis against the security of hardware-accelerated XTS-AES designs.

item.title: Batched Function Secret Sharing: Parallel Generation and Key Compression
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2903
Authors: Tianpei Lu, Keyu Ji, Yuntian Chen, Yuan Zhao, Shoumeng Yan, Bingsheng Zhang, Kui Ren
Summary: Function secret sharing (FSS) enables local evaluation of secret-shared functions and is an important building block for efficient secure computation, particularly for comparisons and private lookups. However, conventional tree-based distributed point functions (DPFs) and distributed comparison functions (DCFs) incur sequential dependencies during key generation and require $O(n\lambda)$-bit keys for fixed output length, where $n$ is the input length and $\lambda$ is the security parameter. We address these bottlenecks through parallel correction-word generation and compact key representation. By sampling the states along the target path in advance, we decouple correction computations across tree levels and enable their parallel generation. For compression, we give a shared-header batch representation under an explicit label-evaluation interface, using homomorphic seed expansion to reconstruct encrypted correction words locally. A uniform sublinear header bound makes the amortized key size approach $n+m$ bits per evaluator per function, where $m$ is the payload length. For 20-bit inputs, parallelization reduces the communication rounds for DPF and DCF from 72 and 1,048, respectively, to 13, while batched FSS requires only one round. Key compression reduces the key size to 1\% of that of conventional FSS schemes and achieves key-generation speedups ranging from $3\times$ to $40\times$.

item.title: Bounds of Falcon's Fast Fourier Sampler with Fixed-Point Arithmetic
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2902
Authors: Vincent Hwang
Summary: Falcon was selected by NIST for standardization as FN-DSA in the forthcoming FIPS 206, and its signature generation is driven by the fast Fourier sampler, defined over the complex numbers. This report bounds the Rényi divergence between the sampler in real arithmetic and its fixed-point implementation, on the tail-cut event, where every sample stays within a fixed number of standard deviations of its center. For a reference bit security λ = 128 at n = 512 and λ = 256 at n = 1024 over 2^64 signatures, the bound keeps 126.28 and 248.78 bits at the plain center, and 126.70 and 253.53 bits at the fractional center, for every key the key generation accepts. The floating-point signer's analysis is left open: it stopped at a numerical contradiction while closing its hypotheses.
We propose four changes to the fixed-point implementation. (i) The one-dimensional sampler SamplerZ rejects a candidate at a saturated shift instead of saturating the shift. (ii) The key generation runs three new checks on the tree: it bounds the largest relative deviation of a leaf standard deviation, the multiplicative perturbation of the tree map, and the largest remainder on the tail-cut event. The first two changes carry the proof: dropping (i) costs the saturated leaves' term, and dropping (ii) leaves no security level at any number of signatures for our proof. (iii) The root node is computed with the NTRU identity, and (iv) an inversion followed by a multiplication becomes a division; these two simplify the proofs.
The bits rest on machine-checked proofs and on three code-alignment hypotheses. The sampler's kernels and its recursion are proved in CryptoLine on the aarch64 objects of the C code, compiled at -O3 and traced under QEMU's Cortex-A72, and composed in Lean. The analysis is carried in Lean where its model reaches, every proof line it does not reach recorded as such, and the Lean theorems take the summability of their series as a hypothesis. The bound samples nothing.
This report was written with agents under the human author's detailed guidance, a blend of formal verification of machine code, the Rényi divergence argument of lattice sampling, and the engineering of an agent harness; the tree map's perturbation is a multiplicative one, in the sense of relative perturbation theory. The compiled objects have known timing side channels: in the key generation's arithmetic the compiler turned constant-time C into key-dependent branches in the Cortex-A72 build, so that arithmetic is verified on the object compiled for the Apple M1, which selects, and a branchless assembly reference is future work with the agents.

item.title: A Bleichenbacher bit-by-bit oracle attack from partial message knowledge
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2901
Authors: Juan Carlos García Escartín
Summary: Oracle attacks show the importance of a correct implementation of cryptographic standards when translated into code. A notable example is the Bleichenbacher attack on RSA with PKCS#1 v1.5 padding and all the improvements that have been suggested over the decades. This paper shows how an attacker knowing a few least significant bytes of an RSA message can take advantage of a server with an oracle side-channel to decrypt the full message bit by bit. We will consider two oracles that can be tested with chosen ciphertexts: one revealing whether the decrypted message starts with the 00 02 bytes and a second one revealing if the decrypted message is fully PKCS compliant. For an attacker knowing the three least significant bytes of the message, the first oracle provides an attack where one oracle call gives the next least significant bit of the message and the second an attack which requires, with high probability, a small constant number of oracle calls to the oracle, with a constant which depends on the length of the message and the desired probability of success. The attack divides the message bits into two sections, one with the known part and one with the unknown part, and then chooses transformations that will keep the unknown part, except for the last unknown bit, orders of magnitude below the integer coming from the known part. The resulting string either gives a valid padding or not depending on the value of the unknown bit. The attacker can minimize the number of oracle calls at the cost of some local computation. Finally, the same method is adapted to show how it can also be used to extract the few least significant bytes of the message with an increased cost where the main complexity is finding a second valid message with a correct padding starting from the original captured ciphertext.

item.title: Modular Walsh rigidity for Boolean functions of degree at most four
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2900
Authors: Filipe Martins Vono, André Oliveira Naufel de Toledo, Valéria Gonzaga Santos
Summary: We establish the sufficient ratio $p/2^m \ge 1/2$ for Boolean functions of algebraic degree at most four in $4m$ variables for every $m \ge 4$. The modulus $p$ is odd and may be composite. If every unnormalized Walsh coefficient is congruent to one of the two bent levels modulo $p$, the function is bent. This removes the dimension cutoff of the previous large-dimension result. The final argument finds an affine zero subspace of the quartic digit in a codimension excluded by the Walsh reductions. It also settles modulus $33$ in $24$ variables.

item.title: Aker: Efficient Two-Party SLH-DSA
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2899
Authors: Yaron Salman, Ben Riva, Dmitry Kogan
Summary: Threshold signing is widely deployed to protect cryptographic keys, but extending these deployments to post-quantum signatures remains challenging. While NIST's lattice-based signatures now have efficient threshold protocols, distributed signing for SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), NIST's stateless hash-based signature standard, has been considered prohibitively expensive because it lacks the algebraic structure those protocols typically exploit.
We present Aker, a maliciously secure two-party signing protocol compatible with an unmodified FIPS 205 verifier. Our approach combines generic secret-sharing MPC with four optimizations that leverage the structure of the SLH-DSA hypertree. Evaluating active layers concurrently collapses sequential hashing depth to that of a single chain. Caching public keys allows authentication paths to be computed locally, so that only the signing leaf is evaluated in MPC. Fixing path prefixes lets signers reuse entire upper-layer signatures across messages. Finally, one-time subtrees sample lower-layer signature components locally rather than deriving them from the secret key, further reducing MPC work. Some of these gains come at the cost of stateful signers and a lower limit on the total number of signatures per key.
We implement and evaluate our protocols using SHAKE-based SLH-DSA in two deployment settings. For server--server deployments, we combine these techniques with a new GPU engine for maliciously secure Boolean GMW. Between two single-GPU servers in separate cloud providers over the public Internet, online signing for SLH-DSA-128f takes $2.09$ seconds, or $0.76$ seconds with a lower signature limit, while input-independent Beaver triple generation runs offline and scales horizontally across keyless CPU workers. For client--server deployments, a periodic offline session prepares a reserve of over a hundred signatures, after which online signing requires only four low-bandwidth communication rounds and local hashing.
These results show that maliciously secure distributed signing for SLH-DSA is within reach today in the two-party setting, while our optimizations extend directly to more parties.

item.title: LEASH: When LaBRADOR’s Guarantees Go Astray
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2898
Authors: Xiang Wang, Ji Xiang
Summary: Succinct arguments enable efficient verification of large computations, while lattice-based constructions offer a promising path toward post-quantum security. LaBRADOR advances this direction through recursive reductions of knowledge that achieve compact proofs. However, these reductions require careful control of witness norms, relation preservation, and knowledge extraction to maintain their claimed guarantees. In this paper, we revisit the correctness and security analysis of LaBRADOR. We construct explicit counterexamples showing that its concrete parameter-selection strategy can fail to preserve completeness, even for valid binary R1CS witnesses. We further identify inconsistencies in recursive relation transformations and inaccuracies in the probability bounds underlying its knowledge extraction analysis. We develop targeted repairs and provide corresponding mathematical analyses, examining how changes to norm bounds, decomposition parameters, and challenge distributions affect the resulting security and efficiency guarantees. Our results highlight the importance of rigorous parameterization and compositional reasoning in lattice-based succinct proof systems.

item.title: Communication-Efficient Threshold-CKKS Aggregation for Secure Cross-Silo Federated Learning
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2897
Authors: Jihyung Kook, Dokyeong Kang, Eunsang Lee
Summary: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative training without sharing raw data, but exchanged model updates may reveal sensitive information. Homomorphic encryption (HE) protects these updates, yet combining collusion resistance, flexible aggregation, dropout handling, and communication efficiency remains challenging. We propose a communication-efficient threshold-CKKS protocol for cross-silo FL with Full and Sparse profiles, without a trusted key-distribution center. Independent local encryption keys enable server-side weighting and dropout-aware reaggregation without ciphertext retransmission. Sparse uses RLWE-MLWE conversion for fine-grained chunk-wise aggregation while retaining compact RLWE packing. Seeded ciphertext reconstruction, selective coefficient transmission, and compressed collective decryption further reduce communication. We establish whole-view simulation security for fixed-cohort executions without dropout or retry against a semi-honest server colluding with up to $c$ clients, under explicitly permitted leakage and a minimum cohort requirement of $\tau\ge c+2$. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 show that Full incurs only 0.32 and 0.29 percentage-point accuracy losses, with 1.78$\times$ and 1.76$\times$ the online communication of plaintext, respectively. At matched accuracy levels, Sparse reduces online communication by factors of approximately 79 and 84 compared with FedPHE. At accuracy targets five percentage points below full-transmission plaintext, Sparse requires only 2.5$\times$ and 2.1$\times$ the online communication of plaintext, respectively. These results narrow the communication gap between encrypted and plaintext FL.

item.title: Four Ciphers in One: Full-Round Attacks on the Reference Implementation of LLBC
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2896
Authors: Sei Kofuku, Yasutaka Igarashi
Summary: LLBC is a 128-bit low-latency block cipher for IoT applications, proposed in the IEEE Internet of Things Journal in 2025. The designers release a reference implementation in C and Verilog for reproducibility. The test vectors in the proposal are outputs of this implementation. We show that the reference implementation differs from the specification of the peer-reviewed proposal in eight points. In particular, its round function uses the rotation amounts $(32,16)$ instead of $(3,19)$. We prove that an LLBC-type cipher with rotation amounts $(b_1,b_2)$ is a product of $g/4$ independent ciphers when $g=\gcd(64,b_1,b_2)$ is a multiple of 4. Hence the cipher splits when $g$ is a multiple of 8. As a result, the reference implementation splits into four 32-bit ciphers that never mix. With this split, we attack all 20 rounds. We give a distinguisher with probability 1 from two chosen plaintexts. We decrypt any ciphertext with $2^{32}$ chosen plaintexts. We recover the master key from three known plaintexts with $2^{80}+3\cdot 2^{16}$ encryptions, which is below exhaustive search by a factor of $2^{48}$. The designers estimated that the best attack on the specification reaches nine rounds. On a single PC, our decryption attack on all 20 rounds of the reference implementation took 175.5 seconds. We also study standard techniques. A standard automatic search returns 20-round impossible differentials and zero-correlation approximations. In contrast, the classical differential and linear characteristics and the integral properties that we examined distinguish only 9, 10, and 8 rounds, respectively, inside one part. We also show that the assumption of the usual models, which treat the S-boxes as independent, does not hold for the reference implementation. Finally, we recommend that designers check the released code against test vectors made independently from the specification and check the diffusion of the released code itself before publication.

item.title: Concrete Quantum Circuit Implementations and Resource Estimates for the Quantum 3 and 4-Sieves
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2895
Authors: MohamadAli Khajeian
Summary: Chailloux and Loyer (2023) introduced quantum 3- and 4-sieve algorithms for the Shortest Vector Problem (SVP) with asymptotic analyses, but concrete circuit implementations remain unexplored. We present the first complete reversible circuits for both algorithms, designing inner-product predicates with signed symmetric squaring across three architectures (low-qubit, balanced, and low-depth). We validate these circuits using exact sparse state-vector simulations that match an independent mathematical model to a precision of \(10^{-13}\). Crucially, we show that the original amplitude-amplification oracle fails when inner Grover searches are approximate and correct it to test the full configuration. Applying our arithmetic techniques to the published NV 2-sieve oracle reduces its T-count by \(9.4-14\times\) and T-depth by over three orders of magnitude. Finally, we provide exact per-call logical resource estimates for the configuration predicates and the NV oracle at cryptographic dimensions, detailing the architectural trade-offs for the core predicates used in quantum tuple sieving.

item.title: BMuSig-L: Blind Multi-Signature from Lattice
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2894
Authors: Anirban Chakraborty, Mriganka Dey, Nikita Dey, Avijit Dutta, Subhabrata Samajder
Summary: Blind signatures and multi-signatures are two fundamental cryptographic primitives for privacy-preserving decentralized protocols. A blind signature enables a user to obtain a signature on a message from a signer while keeping the message hidden from the signer. Moreover, the signer cannot subsequently link the resulting signature to the corresponding signing session. In contrast, a multi-signature scheme allows a group of signers to jointly generate a single signature on a message. Blind multi-signatures, a primitive recently introduced by Karantaidou et al. (AsiaCCS 2024), combine the advantages of both techniques. They enable a user to obtain a joint signature from a group of signers while ensuring that the message remains hidden from every signer and that colluding signers cannot later link the final signature to the corresponding signing session. Recently, Bisht et al. proposed $\textsf{BMuSig2}$ (AsiaCCS 2026), a Schnorr-compatible blind multi-signature scheme whose security is based on the hardness of the discrete logarithm problem. In this paper, we present $\textsf{BMuSig-L}$, a lattice-based, two-round, concurrently secure blind multi-signature scheme. Our construction builds upon the lattice-based multi-signature scheme $\textsf{MuSig-L}$ (CRYPTO 2022), the concurrently secure blind signature scheme of Fuchsbauer and Wolf (CRYPTO 2024), which employs non-interactive zero-knowledge arguments and public-key encryption, and a knowledge-sound non-interactive argument system. We prove that $\textsf{BMuSig-L}$ is one-more unforgeable under the assumptions of the unforgeability of $\textsf{MuSig-L}$, the computational soundness of the underlying non-interactive zero-knowledge proof system, and the knowledge soundness of the employed non-interactive argument of knowledge. Finally, we present a prototype implementation of $\textsf{BMuSig-L}$ and evaluate its performance in terms of signature size and verification time.

item.title: Circulant Diffusion Layers: Cost Bounds and Rectangle Reuse
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2893
Authors: Enyan Li, Gaoli Wang
Summary: We study the addition complexity of sparse invertible circulant matrices over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and odd prime fields. Diffusion is measured by branch numbers, and prime field coefficients are restricted to $\{0,\pm1\}$. Finding optimal general circuits is often difficult, particularly at large matrix orders. Rectangle reuse offers a simpler alternative for explicit circuit construction. We compare the general circuit cost $C_g$ with the rectangle reuse cost $C_{\mathrm{rect}}$, and show that rectangle reuse can approach, and sometimes attain, the general circuit optimum while providing shallow implementations in practical cryptographic parameter settings.
To the best of our knowledge, we establish the first lower bounds on both $C_g$ and $C_{\mathrm{rect}}$ for general matrices in terms of matrix order and branch numbers. We then exploit cyclic structure to obtain cost classifications, sharper bounds, and explicit constructions at minimum weight. Over $\mathbb{F}_2$, we give a complete classification of rectangle costs over all invertible weight-three circulants and determine their exact minima at every order $n\ge4$. The minimum costs in both the general circuit and rectangle reuse models equal $3n/2$ at every even order, with connected constructions attaining these minima. Over every odd prime field, connected weight-three constructions likewise attain both minima, namely $\lceil3n/2\rceil$, for every $n\ge4$. For branch number five, we prove the rectangle lower bound $2n$ and give connected families attaining it at infinitely many orders. For branch number six, we exploit cyclic structure to sharpen the general rectangle bounds and determine certified exact rectangle minima at selected orders. Finally, we characterize the effects of connectivity and circuit depth. For weight-three circulants over $\mathbb{F}_2$ or $\mathbb{F}_p$ with $p\ge5$, the minimum gate count at depth two equals the rectangle cost. These results provide theoretical cost benchmarks and explicit constructions for designing circulant diffusion layers with low gate counts and shallow circuits.

item.title: Phase-Hiding Programmable Bootstrapping with Online Client Assistance
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2892
Authors: Xingke Chai
Summary: Programmable bootstrapping in Fast Fully Homomorphic Encryption over the Torus (TFHE) uses a bootstrapping key (BSK) to control successive external products during blind rotation, incurring computational cost and introducing and propagating error. We introduce Phase-Hiding Programmable Bootstrapping (PH-PBS), in which the key-holding client precomputes single-use phase tokens encrypting randomly shifted monomials and assists refresh online. Through phase sharing and a small garbled circuit, the parties compute a masked rotation correction that lets the server align a token for lookup, replacing BSK-driven blind rotation. Using the aligned monomial, the server evaluates private lookup tables, retains ciphertexts for further computation, and delivers only prescribed terminal plaintexts to the client. To reduce token preparation and transmission costs, we construct a projection independent of table values that, under matched randomness and quantization, produces the same complete learning-with-errors (LWE) output ciphertext as the full quantized-token path, coefficientwise. We analyze error propagation in both fixed key-switching orders and derive numerical failure-probability bounds for finite sequential tasks with fixed public schedules and shared key-switching material, under the specified finite-precision model and conditional on successful initialization. Under the stated cryptographic assumptions, we simulate each party's complete session view in the classical static semi-honest model and bound the distinguishing advantage. On a four-bit workload where PH-PBS and the TFHE-rs baseline both use 32-bit coefficients in their key-switching keys and matched decomposition parameters, mean local refresh time with pre-core key switching decreases from 18.392 ms to 3.713 ms, a 79.8% reduction, including both parties' computation and consumed-token preparation. Separate measurements with pre-core key switching place PH-PBS's normalized core-output error variance at approximately one three-thousandth of the corresponding baseline variance. Across the examined modes and network scenarios, estimated refresh-stage times are 46.3%–80.1% lower than those of the corresponding TFHE-rs baselines; these estimates assume serial computation and communication, completed initialization, and sufficient initial correlated oblivious-transfer material.

item.title: Multiparty Computation with Minimal Overhead without Circuit Transformation
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2891
Authors: Aditya Hegde, Phuoc Van Long Pham, Mingyuan Wang
Summary: A central goal in secure multiparty computation (MPC) is to minimize the gap between the total computation performed by all parties and the cost of insecure circuit evaluation. In the honest majority setting, the ideal overhead of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(1)$ is known to be achievable. However, all prior protocols over prime fields attaining this goal for general circuits relied on the so-called share packing techniques and, as a consequence, required prohibitively expensive circuit transformation steps to impose repetitive structure on the circuit.
The only exception is the recent work of Garg, Jain, Mukherjee, and Wang (CRYPTO’24), which introduced a share unpacking technique and obtained the first such protocol without circuit transformation. However, their protocol only applies when the underlying field size is extraordinarily large, in particular, exponential in the *square* of the number of parties.
In this work, we present the first MPC protocol with $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(1)$ overhead for any prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$ (more generally, any integer ring $\mathbb{Z}_p$) whose size is only required to be $n^{\Omega(n)}$, where $n$ is the number of parties (as opposed to $n^{\Omega(n^2)}$). Technically, we extend the unpacking approach of Garg et al. by developing a new approach to linear randomness extraction over integers, a tool that may be of independent interest.

item.title: Byzantine Agreement with Signature Tokens
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2890
Authors: Yuval Efron, Mahimna Kelkar, Saachi Mutreja, Tim Roughgarden
Summary: We investigate the power and limitations of quantum cryptography in distributed consensus protocols. Specifically, we study the fundamental problem of Byzantine Agreement in partial synchrony, in a setting in which each party has access to a finite number $k$ of signature tokens. Classically, this problem is solvable only when less than one-third of the parties can be faulty (Dwork, Lynch, Stockmeyer 1988). We prove that protocols with signature tokens can bypass this lower bound by designing a protocol that remains secure against up to a $\frac{2^{k+1}-1}{2^{k+2}-1}$-fraction of faults. In particular, with $k=\Theta(\log n)$, where $n$ denotes the number of parties, our protocol solves Byzantine Agreement in partial synchrony assuming only an honest majority. Conversely, we prove that $\Omega(\log n)$ signature tokens are necessary for such a result. Finally, for $k=1$, we prove that the fault-tolerance threshold of $3/7$ achieved by our protocol is the best possible.

item.title: Quadratic APN Functions of $\mathbb{F}_2^{10}$ with a Self-Equivalence of Prime Order
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2889
Authors: Emanuele Bellini
Summary: Almost perfect nonlinear (APN) functions of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ have the lowest possible differential uniformity. The only known APN permutation in even dimension, in dimension six, is equivalent to a quadratic APN function with a nontrivial linear self-equivalence; no APN permutation is known for even $n \geq 8$. In a published collection of about 3.8 million quadratic APN classes of dimension eight, at most 0.34% have a nontrivial linear self-equivalence. In dimension ten, the 25 literature classes considered here all have one. We study all quadratic APN functions of $\mathbb{F}_2^{10}$ with such a self-equivalence, which usually confines them to a much smaller linear space. Up to conjugacy and power similarity, self-equivalences of prime order have 299 types. We settle 298 of them. Elementary lemmas exclude 280 types, and exhaustive searches confirm this for 242 of them. The other 18 types are settled by exhaustive searches with exact equivalence certificates. Up to extended affine equivalence, the 298 types contain 29 classes of quadratic APN functions, four of them new. This also classifies the quadratic APN functions with coefficients in a subfield. Exactly 24 classes contain one with coefficients in $\mathbb{F}_4$, and all 3 that contain one with coefficients in $\mathbb{F}_{32}$ are among them. The open type consists of the quadratic canonical triplicate functions. They correspond to maximum additive Hermitian rank-distance codes. Three different searches find only the invariants of 16 classes, all among the 29. We conjecture there are no others. No quadratic APN function in the 298 settled types is Carlet-Charpin-Zinoviev equivalent to a permutation.

item.title: FALCON-PARE: Full-Range Side-Channel Key Recovery of Falcon via Prior-Enhanced Evidence
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2888
Authors: Shuyi Chen, Yuejun Liu, Jingdian Ming, Wei Cheng, Yuhan Zhao, Yongbin Zhou
Summary: Falcon is a compact post-quantum signature scheme selected by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), and its number-theoretic transform (NTT) computations constitute a critical side-channel attack surface. Existing NTT attacks rely on truncated coefficient ranges and do not cover the full valid range of Falcon secret coefficients, limiting their applicability to complete key recovery. This paper proposes FALCON-PARE, a prior-enhanced evidence framework for full-range key recovery of Falcon. FALCON-PARE combines Falcon's discrete-Gaussian prior with aggregated leakage from range conversion and Montgomery multiplication to construct input-layer soft evidence, which is propagated through the NTT factor graph. FALCON-PARE further uses posterior entropy to select reliable coefficients and public-key relation to complete the remaining unknowns, yielding full recovery of the secret polynomials f and g. We systematically evaluate FALCON-PARE on STM32F407 under -O0 and -O3 compiler settings, validating its practicality in terms of profiling-trace requirements, coefficient-wise accuracy, and residual candidate-space reduction. FALCON-PARE achieves single-trace full key recovery with 40 and 120 profiling traces, respectively. At the comparison budgets, FALCON-PARE achieves absolute gains of 54.79% and 73.83% in coefficient-wise accuracy over existing soft-analytical side-channel attacks (SASCA) for NTT leakage, and reduces the residual candidate space from approximately \(2^{4352}\) and \(2^{5346}\) to one, respectively.

item.title: Homomorphic Encryption and Bootstrapping for Real Matrices over Conjugate-Invariant Rings
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2887
Authors: Ilaria Chillotti, Hyojun Kim, Yeongmin Lee, Yongwoo Lee, Damien Ligier
Summary: The conjugate-invariant variant of CKKS (CI-CKKS) by Kim and Song encrypts real vectors over the subring of a power-of-two cyclotomic ring fixed by $X \mapsto X^{-1}$, with as many real slots as the rank of the ring. The Gentry–Lee scheme (GL) packs batches of complex matrices into a three-variable ring and multiplies them natively. GL bootstrapping replaces the rotations of the slot transforms with ciphertext–plaintext matrix products. We combine the two lines of work. First, we give a bootstrapping procedure for CI-CKKS: its transforms factor the real decoding matrix into sparse stages, and its modular reduction runs only once, on real slots, and needs no conjugation key. Second, by folding the three GL variables under their inversions, we obtain three subrings that have real slots and are closed under the matrix product; they define $\mathsf{CI}^{1}\text{-}\mathsf{GL}$, $\mathsf{CI}^{2}\text{-}\mathsf{GL}$, and $\mathsf{CI}^{3}\text{-}\mathsf{GL}$. We describe $\mathsf{CI}^{3}\text{-}\mathsf{GL}$ in detail: it encrypts real matrices, needs no conjugation, and, for the same matrix size and number of matrices, has keys of half the rank of GL keys. Third, we adapt the matrix-product bootstrapping of GL to $\mathsf{CI}^{3}\text{-}\mathsf{GL}$. We prototyped these techniques.

item.title: Round-Key Equivalence and Collisions of the Revised MoFang
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2886
Authors: Zhang zhihong, Liu fengyaxuan
Summary: The revised reference implementation of MoFang moves the S-box of the second message half to row 1, which does not eliminate the original per-round key cancellation. Collisions of this type on the original version have been independently reported2,3; this paper does not repeat those findings, and instead proves for the revised version that when the nonzero words of that half are confined to three designated positions, the full message expansion preserves the per-round cancellation, so that every input has 16 round-key-equivalent inputs. The property holds for any common chaining value and transfers to the complete behavior of the six reference variants under full padding, fixed initialization, and XOF output interfaces. Furthermore, the sufficient condition is promoted to a complete classification of the round key map: the common difference of any two equivalent inputs must belong to the original 16 period-two masks, and the equivalence class sizes can only be 1, 2, 4, or 16, with size 16 corresponding exactly to the original domain D0. For the DM variants, necessary and sufficient conditions for all nontrivial equivalence classes are given, together with an exact integer count of the covered domain (log2 ≈ 814.04647); the domain covered by equivalence classes of size at least four admits a three-state matrix counting formula. These results char acterize the equivalence of complete round-key sequences; the domain sizes do not indicate running time or security strength. The object of study is fixed to the 64-bit word model corresponding to the public submission; mathematical proofs, computer-assisted counting, and experimental verification against the reference C code are stated separately.

item.title: Revisiting homomorphic AES evaluation with Hybrid Byte-Bit Packing
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2885
Authors: Lu Zhang, Xuan Shen, Ruida Wang, Xianhui Lu, Yin Zhang, Chao Li, Shaojing Fu
Summary: Homomorphic AES evaluation is an important benchmark for practical FHE systems. Existing BGV-based AES transciphering schemes typically employ byte-oriented representations, which are well suited for exploiting the algebraic structure of the multiplicative inversion in the SubBytes operation. However, evaluating the affine transformation and subsequent linear layers in this representation introduces additional automorphisms and key-switching operations. In this work, we propose a hybrid byte-bit packing strategy for efficient BGV-based AES transciphering. After performing the multiplicative inversion in the SubBytes operation, we introduce an unpacking procedure to convert the slot packing scheme from byte-oriented to bit-oriented. The affine transformation in SubBytes and subsequent AES linear transformations are unified and evaluated over GF(2) using homomorphic additions, avoiding the key-switching operations involved in the packed byte-oriented evaluation of these linear components. We further optimize the unpacking procedure using a hoisting technique, achieving a 2.5× speedup in unpacking latency compared with the non-hoisted implementation. We implement our approach in HElib and evaluate it under parameters satisfying at least 128-bit security. Experimental results demonstrate per-block latency speedups of 2.6× and 11.7× without bootstrapping, and 2.1× and 3.3× with bootstrapping, on a local machine and a 64-thread server, respectively, compared with the reproduced BGV-based AES baseline under the same software, hardware, and security settings.

item.title: A Note on Non-interactive Deniable Secret Sharing from Indistinguishability Obfuscation
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2884
Authors: Shafik Nassar
Summary: Deniable secret sharing, introduced by Canetti et al. (TCC 2025), protects shareholders when a subset of them is coerced into revealing their shares. Namely, a set of fakers can produce fake shares that are consistent with a fake secret of their choice, and that are indistinguishable from real shares. Very recently, Amores et al. (TCC 2026) studied deniable secret sharing in a setting where the fakers cannot interact to produce their fake shares. Specifically, each faker locally computes its fake share given only its own share, the set of fakers, and the fake secret. Their constructions of non-interactive deniable secret sharing either have shares of exponential size or rely on virtual black-box obfuscation.
We show how to upgrade any secret sharing scheme, for any access structure, into a non-interactive deniable secret sharing scheme using a collusion-resistant constrained PRF with static security, which can be instantiated from polynomially-secure indistinguishability obfuscation and one-way functions. Our transformation incurs an additive share size overhead that is polynomial in the number of shareholders. By using indistinguishability obfuscation directly, together with a somewhere-statistically binding hash, we further reduce the overhead to polylogarithmic in the number of shareholders. In combination with prior work on succinct computational secret sharing, we get succinct deniable secret sharing from indistinguishability obfuscation and standard assumptions.

item.title: Early-Stopping Dishonest Majority Broadcast with Optimal Round Complexity
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2883
Authors: Renas Bacho, Kecheng Shi
Summary: Early-stopping broadcast protocols guarantee termination as a function of the number $f\le t$ of parties actually corrupted in an execution, rather than of the worst-case bound $t<2\min\{t,n-2\}$, a condition that covers a broad part of the dishonest-majority regime. It has remained open whether this bound can be attained, even at the cost of exponential communication.
In this work, we present a deterministic early-stopping broadcast protocol in which every honest party outputs and terminates within $\min\{f+3,t+1\}$ rounds for every $t<n$. The protocol is built from exponential information gathering (EIG) graphs and incurs exponential communication. It works in the plain PKI model with idealized signatures and is secure against a strongly adaptive adversary. Its stopping round complexity is therefore optimal throughout the stated range of the lower bound.

item.title: Limits of Pseudorandom Codes under Adaptive Corruption
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2882
Authors: Ganyuan Cao
Summary: Pseudorandom codes (PRCs) hide messages in strings that look uniformly random to anyone without the decoder key. If the key may be stolen after some codewords have been sent, security requires that these codewords and the stolen key be indistinguishable from uniform strings, chosen independently of the messages, together with a key that decodes each of them to its message. We call producing such a key \emph{opening} the codewords, and ask how many key bits it takes.
We first show that every adaptively secure PRC yields a \emph{$q$-use code} with the same key length, namely its opened key together with the $q$ uniform strings it opens. Lower bounds for these information-theoretic objects therefore hold unconditionally and apply to every adaptively secure PRC, including current designs based on hardness assumptions.
We then show that every opening costs key bits beyond the opened message: $\omega(\log\lambda)$ without errors, $\frac{1}{\rho^2}\cdot\omega(\log\lambda)$ under random noise of correlation $\rho$, and, for every alphabet, a constant fraction of the codeword if every error pattern up to a constant fraction of the length must be corrected, even when an unbounded adversary chooses it with the key. We call the last cost the robustness tax. As for non-committing encryption, adaptively secure PRCs thus need an a-priori bound on the number of openings, but each opening costs more, because of the tension between soundness and robustness: a sound key must reject almost all strings, yet accept a region around each uniformly random codeword. We show simple stateful codes meet these bounds and yield stateful PRCs with perfect bounded adaptive security.
Finally, unlike for non-committing encryption, a programmable random oracle cannot pay this cost under noise. Errors move the decoder's queries away from any programmed point, so for decoders with non-adaptive oracle queries, every opening must still be paid for in key bits or in programmed points that the decoder reads on a noticeable fraction of inputs.

item.title: RRHL: A Relational Logic for Rényi Differential Privacy of Private Learning
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2881
Authors: Gilles Barthe, Davide Davoli
Summary: Differential privacy is the standard framework for defining privacy-preserving computation and is adopted in large-scale production systems, including industrial-level private learning. The underlying algorithms are based on complex privacy-enhancing mechanisms such as privacy amplification by subsampling and correlated noising. Proving their privacy requires advanced reasoning techniques such as the moments accountant and shifted composition; no existing approach to formal verification supports all of them. In this work, we introduce RRHL: a relational program logic for proving Rényi differential privacy of imperative programs with continuous sampling instructions. Its judgments express bounds on the privacy budgets of instructions as functions of the program states, and its composition of budgets is sharp. We use RRHL to prove differential privacy of the algorithms widely implemented and deployed. These include several variants of DP-SGD and DP-FTRL, and gradient descent with per-record Rényi filters. In several cases the bounds match the best known Rényi differential privacy analyses. The logic, its soundness proof and the case studies are formalized in Lean. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first formal privacy analysis, via a relational program logic, of private learning algorithms with state-of-the-art Rényi differential privacy bounds.

item.title: Sum-Checking SmallWood: Smaller Hash-Based Zero-Knowledge Arguments
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2880
Authors: Thibauld Feneuil, Killian Provin, Matthieu Rivain
Summary: Hash-based zero-knowledge (ZK) arguments are particularly attractive for their conservative post-quantum security, relying only on cryptographic hash functions. While VOLE-in-the-Head proofs, based on GGM trees, are the most compact for very small witnesses, Merkle-tree-based approaches take over for larger ones. In this regime, the recent SmallWood scheme achieves the smallest proof sizes for witness sizes ranging from $2^6$ to $2^{16}$.
In this work, we present SmallWood+, an enhanced variant of SmallWood that leverages sum-check-based protocols to further reduce proof sizes. Following the paradigm of Longfellow ZK, where a hash-based ZK argument is used to wrap the verification of a sum-check-based protocol, we formalize the notion of Sum-Check Verification Constraint System (SVCS), which captures a broad class of such protocols, including GKR for layered circuits and the sum-check protocol for R1CS. We then design generic compilers transforming SVCS instances into ZK arguments from linear commitment schemes and/or multilinear polynomial commitment schemes, which we efficiently instantiate from SmallWood.
Along the way, we develop tools of independent interest: hiding multilinear extensions, which make a multilinear evaluation of the committed witness safe to reveal in the small-field regime, a zero-knowledge version of the ring-switching protocol, and an improved circuit-flattening technique for GKR.
Applied to (layered) arithmetic circuits, hash functions, and lattice-based statements, our constructions establish new state-of-the-art proof sizes for hash-based ZK arguments - for instance, 18 KB and 63 KB to prove 1 and 100 Keccak permutations, against 29 KB and 127 KB for the best previous schemes.

item.title: Privacy-Preserving Systemic Portfolio Analysis and Repair
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2879
Authors: Martin Zbudila, Roozbeh Sarenche, Aysajan Abidin, Bart Preneel
Summary: Financial institutions can be exposed to systemic risk through overlapping portfolios and common liquidity shocks, yet identifying and reducing these dependencies requires precisely the portfolio information that institutions are unwilling to reveal. We present, to the best of our knowledge, the first privacy-preserving framework combining system -level portfolio analysis with coordinated portfolio repair. Our approach uses secure multi-party computation (MPC), allowing mutually distrustful institutions to jointly identify systemic vulnerabilities and determine concrete portfolio adjustments without disclosing their underlying holdings. We provide both an MPC realization and a federated variant that moves fund-local computation outside MPC while retaining secure global coordination, and we analyze the additional leakage introduced by this federated design. We implement and evaluate the complete framework on real, publicly available portfolios. Across representative network profiles, private analysis completes in roughly 1–4 minutes and portfolio repair takes 2.6–8.8 hours in MPC and 13–21 minutes in the federated setting. Our results show that both private systemic-risk analysis and coordinated intervention are practically feasible with current MPC technology.

item.title: Batch, Pack, and Prove: More Efficient Verifiable Computation for CKKS
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2878
Authors: Ignacio Cascudo, Anamaria Costache, Daniele Cozzo, Dario Fiore, Antonio Guimarães, Eduardo Soria-Vazquez
Summary: An important challenge in homomorphic encryption (HE) is ensuring the integrity of the encrypted computations. Although verifiable computation can address this in theory, making it practical is far from trivial. [Cascudo et al. CRYPTO 2025] recently proposed a solution to this problem for the CKKS scheme. In particular, they propose new succinct arguments that efficiently prove arithmetic circuits and range checks over the ring $R_q = \mathbb{Z}_q[Y]/(Y^N+1)$, and combine them to prove computations on CKKS ciphertexts. Despite the important progress, their work faces scalability challenges: the size of the polynomial commitment proofs, a large $O(N)$ overhead in range proofs, and the lack of an explicit method for efficient -- sublinear in circuit size -- verification. In this paper we present new techniques that remove all these bottlenecks. First, we provide a more efficient arithmetization of CKKS computations. Second, we introduce BatchFold, a new polynomial commitment for $R_q$ that supports batched evaluations and achieves shorter proofs. Third, we design packing, a novel algebraic technique that eliminates the need to commit to massive polynomials and removes the $O(N)$ overhead in range proofs. Finally, we introduce SparsePack, an efficient protocol for proving the evaluations of sparse, circuit-dependent polynomials, leveraging both packing and batched evaluations. We evaluate the efficiency of our solution on a generic neural network architecture, achieving proofs several orders of magnitude smaller and faster than prior approaches.

item.title: Toward Eﬃcient Post-Quantum Bitcoin Bridges
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2877
Authors: Stephen Duan, Vanhger Pham, Blake Hou, Ethan Zhu, Jingping Yin
Summary: BitVM-style protocols verify succinct proofs on Bitcoin by garbling a proof veriﬁer oﬀ-chain. What reaches the chain in a dispute is the proof itself: its bits under one-time keys, the scripts that authenticate them and the signatures that bind them to transactions. Existing designs garble elliptic-curve succinct non-interactive argument of knowledge (SNARK) veriﬁers, which a quantum adversary breaks. Our goal is a post-quantum alternative: a hash-based scalable transparent argument of knowledge (STARK) veriﬁer, garbled and fed with hash-based one-time keys, with no number-theoretic assumption anywhere in the veriﬁer; its price is a far larger proof, and this paper measures and reduces that on-chain data. We compile the complete veriﬁer for WHIR-based STARK proofs from Ziren into a Boolean circuit using free-XOR gadgets for binary-tower arithmetic and Blake3. Our implementation uses Ziren’s binary-ﬁeld proof stage and narrow recursion. For an Ethereum block proved through four recursion levels, the ﬁnal recursive WHIR-proof veriﬁer has 175.4M non-free gates and 520,832 input bits, corresponding to 2.81 GB of garbled tables, and publishing that input with translated Winternitz keys takes 3.93 million virtual bytes (MvB), in 41 standard transactions. The costs are coupled: on-chain cost grows linearly with the input bits, oﬀ-chain storage with the gate count, and proving time exponentially with the grinding that shortens the input. The WHIR schedule, the Merkle cap depth and the input encoding trade these costs against one another, and a model of proof size and proving time selects the setting, a step toward practical post-quantum Bitcoin bridges.

item.title: Encrypted Authorship Attribution for Fraud Detection
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2876
Authors: Zita Baronnet, Leonard Schild
Summary: Authorship attribution techniques are routinely used to re- late anonymous or disputed texts to known authors through characteris- tic writing styles. Within the financial sector, such techniques may sup- port investigations of phishing campaigns, impersonation attempts, in- vestment scams, or other forms of fraud. More concretely, these methods can be leveraged to determine whether newly observed communications are linked to previously identified actors. In practice, however, both the communications under investigation and the intelligence databases used for attribution may contain sensitive information that cannot be shared across organizational boundaries. In this work, we investigate the privacy-preserving evaluation of sty- lometric authorship attribution through fully homomorphic encryption (FHE). We focus on Burrows’ Delta, a widely studied authorship attribu- tion method based on token frequency statistics and z-score comparisons. We present a homomorphic implementation of Burrows’ Delta, describe a motivating fraud-analysis scenario together with its threat model and trust assumptions, and then analyze the resulting computational com- plexity. Finally, we evaluate the practicality of the proposed approach us- ing the CKKS homomorphic encryption scheme and show that the com- plete pipeline can be executed without bootstrapping while maintaining high numerical accuracy. Our results demonstrate that stylometric au- thorship attribution constitutes a realistic target for privacy-preserving outsourced analytics and illustrate how homomorphic encryption can support confidential fraud investigations.

item.title: Security Analysis of Anonymous Authentication in Apple's Private Cloud Compute
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2875
Authors: Callista Gratz, Anja Lehmann, Andrey Sidorenko
Summary: Apple's Private Cloud Compute (PCC) offloads on-device computation, such as large language-model prompts, to the cloud while seeking to preserve the privacy users expect from local processing. At its core lies a custom authentication protocol that must reconcile three competing goals: restricting access to registered users within a rate limit, doing so without revealing user identities or linking their requests, and nonetheless retaining the ability to hold misbehaving users accountable. Apple's protocol combines blind RSA signatures in a hierarchical issuance with a salted-hash binding trick, but ships without any formal statement -- let alone proof -- of the guarantees it is meant to provide. In this work we close this gap by abstracting the desired authentication protocol as PORTA -- pseudonymously openable, rate-limited tokens for anonymous authentication. We formally define the desired privacy, security, and abuse-mitigation properties such a protocol should satisfy, including a new binding notion specific to the protocol's two-step issuance. We then cast Apple's protocol in this model and show that it achieves the rate-limiting goal and, with a small modification, all privacy goals. Its abuse-mitigation mechanism, which is not yet active in the deployed system, would however not provide the desired accountability guarantees even once enabled. Finally, we present an alternative construction based on anonymous credentials that provably achieves all properties and verifies the binding of tokens already at the gateway, so that a user's pseudonym is only revealed in case of abuse.

item.title: Triads below the ISA: Optimizing Cryptographic Software in CPU Microcode
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2874
Authors: Sabrina Manickam, Rowan Fimmano, Peter Schwabe, Yuval Yarom
Summary: Cryptographic software is typically optimized for the instruction set architecture exposed by the processor. Modern processors, however, contain deeper execution layers with computational capabilities and constraints that differ from those of the instruction set architecture (ISA). This work explores the programmable microcode layer in x86 as an implementation target. We characterize the microcode domain as a distinct target architecture for cryptographic computation and adapt implementations to the state, operations, invocation interface, capacity, and scheduling resources it exposes. We instantiate this methodology on Intel Goldmont with Keccak f [1600] and X25519, two case studies with substantially different computational structures. Our Keccak implementation reduces permutation latency by 7.36% relative to the fastest native implementation in our comparison, with the improvement remaining visible in incomplete SHA3-256 computations. For X25519, our microcode multiplication and squaring kernels free the multiplier from fixed operand registers and restrictive carry-flag semantics, outperforming the native implementations we evaluate. The resulting complete X25519 implementation requires 7.3% fewer cycles than s2n-bignum and 9.8% fewer cycles than OpenSSL. Together, these results demonstrate that looking below the ISA exposes a distinct design space for cryptographic implementation and provide a systematic methodology for exploring it.

item.title: Optimized Solving Strategy and Two-Step Estimator for LWE with Hints
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2873
Authors: Hanbin Yang, Jinzheng Cao, Risheng Yin, Qingfeng Cheng
Summary: Side-channel hints can reduce the cost of solving the Learning with Errors (LWE) problem. We optimize a two-step strategy for LWE with hints that uses BKZ reduction followed by final lattice sieving. Given a lattice constructed from the hints and a specified pair of reduction and sieving algorithms, the strategy jointly selects BKZ block sizes, tour counts, and a final sieving configuration. We also introduce a two-step estimator that predicts the reduced-basis profile and estimates the probability of secret recovery. We combine these estimates with cost models to select a strategy that meets the success-probability and resource constraints. Experiments show that our strategy significantly outperforms the methods of Cao et al. (CRYPTO 2025) and May and Nowakowski (ASIACRYPT 2023). For example, using BLASterBKZ for lattice reduction and the BGJ sieve for final sieving, our strategy recovers the secret for a CRYSTALS-KYBER 512 instance with 190 perfect hints in 7 minutes, compared with 1.6 hours reported by Cao et al. and 7.4 hours reported by May and Nowakowski. With 64 threads, our strategy recovers the secret with 170 perfect hints in 82 minutes. These results highlight the importance of accounting for side-channel leakage when assessing lattice-based cryptographic schemes.

item.title: On the Security of the Cubic UOV Variant CML
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2872
Authors: Manit Gupta
Summary: CML is a cubic multivariate signature scheme proposed over $\mathbb{F}_q$ with $q = 2^8$. Earlier cubic Oil--Vinegar variants such as CUOV and CSSv were broken by differential and high-rank attacks. CML adds an $\ell$-invertible cycle system and a secret position-hiding map to hide the cubic positions. We show that the cubic homogeneous parts of the public key span a space of dimension at most two, so a publicly derived output combination has degree at most two. After restriction to the oil-direction space, the polar matrices of the publicly derived quadratic components span rank-two matrices associated with the edges of a path. This structure yields a procedure for recovering an equivalent key. Our implementation recovered an equivalent key in under 5~minutes for each tested parameter set, including the set targeting 256-bit security.

item.title: The Price of Geometry for Private Distance-Sensitive Filters: $\ell_\infty$ versus $\ell_2$
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2871
Authors: Paul Cesaretti
Summary: A distance-sensitive set representation stores a set $S$ in a metric space and must accept points within distance $r$ of $S$ and reject points farther than $cr$, each with error probability at most $\alpha$. Under differential privacy, even exact membership costs a privacy loss of $\ln(1/\alpha)$; we ask how much \emph{more} the geometry of the space forces. Earlier lower bounds cover only restricted mechanisms, such as partition-based ones or those whose outputs contain no scattered false positives (``dust''). We prove lower bounds for every mechanism.
In $\ell_\infty^d$ with $c<3$ the extra cost is $\Theta_c(d)$, which proves a recent conjecture in this range; when $\lfloor cr\rfloor-r+1$ divides $2r$, a randomly shifted grid is optimal up to $\tilde O(\alpha)$ per dimension. In $\ell_2^d$ the extra cost is instead $\Theta_c(\min(d,\ln(1/\alpha)))$: a new mechanism that outputs a single very large ball shows that dimensions beyond about $\ln(1/\alpha)$ are free, so partition-based constructions are optimal in $\ell_\infty$ but not in $\ell_2$.
